PRAYER.
Our Father in Heaven ! we come to Thee this day because we love
Thee. We come to Thee because we would worship Thee. We come
to Thee individually, and we pray Thee that Thou wilt make us true
and brave and strong and wise and good. We come to Thee collectively, as members of this Great Fraternity, and we pray Thee that Thou
wilt give us wisdom and strength and courage and gnidance. W c pray
Thee that our influence for good may he as broad as the wide world.
We pray Thee that our sympathies may be as deep as human need, and
we pray Thee that our service to our fellow men on earth may be
pleasing and acceptable in Thy sight. We pray Thee that this Grand
Lodge, thus begun in order, may be conducted in peace and closed in
perfect harmony. In the name of Him whose life on earth was the
perfect example of brotherly love, relief and truth; in the name of Him
who taught us to say, Our Father, we ask it. Amen.

Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
The ceremony in which you have just participated has opened with
amplified detail the Sixty-fifth Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of California, and it becomes my duty, agreeably to the requirements of the constitution, to acquaint you with such acts as I have
performed in fulfilling the trust imposed upon me as your chiet executive officer at the last Communication of this Grand Lodge, as well
as give you such information as I have relative to the general welfare
of the craft, and such suggestions as to legislation and other matters
as will tend to promote the fundamental principles of Free Masonry,
to the end that the membership may enjoy a greater fruition as we
pass from the accomplished things of the past to the possibilities of
the future.
,
Masonry has never been content to rest upon the laurels of past
achievement, splendiclly as that stands out in its history and tradition.
It has an "unhasting unresting," never-ending work to accomplish in
its chosen mission to elevate mankind. That there is ample work to
accomplish is pitifully evidenced by the unspeakable calamity that
now overshadows the greater part of the civilized world. The accomplishment of t.he dream of the idealist for peace on earth, good will
to men, that seemed so near of realization in the first generation of
the twentieth century, is as absolutely impossible as at any time in
the most brutal ages of the world's history. It was to be hoped
that under the guidance of an all-wise directing Master the influence
of the millions of our craft who stood for the fatherhood of God and
the brotherhood of man, such a stupendous calamity might have been
averted. But such was not to be, and it only the more forcibly reminds us of our solemn responsibilities. The fight is not lost, but
only stayed. In the end justice and right and eternal truth mnst prevail, and in the accomplishment of that grand mission Free Masonry
must and will play not only an important part, but it should be the
most important role; and I sincerely trust and hope and pray that
the beneficent influence of the teachings of our great institution will so
permeate the citizenship of this great nation that a repetition of this
stupendous calamity may never he the fate of the people of this continent; certain!>· the example of its appalling tragedy must inevitably
make the teachings of Masonry more effective, and the probability of
its recurrence less probable, and in this connection we should express
our thanks to Almighty God that there stands at the helm of state a
man that inspires the confidence of security and fills us with an abicl-

I feel it incumbent upon me at this time to call your attention to the necessity of taking some action relative to the relief
of the terrible suffering and misery that necessarily follow in the wake
of the fearful cataclysm that embraces practically all the nations of
Europe. There is no doubt hut that in the immediate future the Grand
jurisdictions on this continent will he called upon to take concerted
action. In such a movement the loyalty of California to the sacred precepts of our Institution and her sympathy with the pitiful calls of
suffering humanity will be exemplified in no uncertain manner. This
is a vital and impcrati,·c matter-a matte.r of tremendous magnitude,
and the solution calls for serious and conscientious consideration. The
suffering and distress engendered by the monumental struggle has had
no counterpart in the history of the world's warfare. Thousandshundreds of thousands of those who are helplessly depen9cnt are the
immediate families of tho;;e who have assumed our vows and burdens
and responsibilities. and arc entitled to our benefits and privileges. One
of the first and most important lessons of the craft declares in no uncertain terms that l\Tasonic charity recognizes no limitation of country
or clime. In order that this matter may be brought to the consideration of the Grand Lodge, I have appointed a special committee of three,
consisting of Past Grand Master Charles L. Patton, Otto L. Sues and
Dozier Finley, to formulate such a plan of action as will appeal to their
discretion and meet the requirements of the situation, and present the
same in the form of a report to this Grand Lodge.
This has been a l~anner year for Pree Masonry in California. The
reports in the hands of the Grand Secretary show a greater increase
of membership than that of any antecedent year in our history. Thirteen dispensations for the formation of new lodges have been issued,
and in this respect also exceeding all previous records. This is as it
should be. Onr wonderful Empire of the West is advancing in wealth
and population as no other commonwealth in the Union, and it is hut
natural that this gr cat fraternity should keep pace in the general uphl'ilding. I hope that the growth has been natural and healthy. In my
visitations throughout the state I have endeavored to impress upon the
membership that ~lasonry is not a reformatory. nor an institution that
recognizes mere- monetary stringency as a justillcation for accepting
1111desirable timber. There is nothing more antagonistic to Masonic
teaching and more disgusting to real l\Iasons than the sugg-estion that
keen rivalry and small treasuries will justify promotion hy "drumming"
up carnlidatcs. The character of the men who have assembled in the
lodge rooms and at the banquet tables in the scver;t! l\f:io;onic districts

...

It is surprising to one who has made no ir~vestigation how slight
is the criminal clement in our Masonic membership as disclosed by the
number in this Jurisdiction against whom charges for criminal offenses,
Masonic or otherwise, have been preferred. Less than one in evcrv
twenty-five hundred Masons in California is prosecuted for crimes in·volving moral turpitude in the tribunals of the order, and little more
than <;>ne-half pf that number are actually found guilty ancl disciplined.
This, of course, includes all prosecutions, whether for offenses designated as purely Masonic offenses, or violations of the penal statutes of
the state. While there is in some lodges. no doubt, a reluctance to
prosecute and a tendency to minimize. I feel confident that there are
in every lodge those whose con;cientions devotion to dutv would not
permit them to let those who have seriously offended • against our
laws escape the just consequences of their acts. Judged hy this practical standard of actual experience. we may safely conclude that our
lodges are living up faithfully to the traditions of our institution in
maintaining the highest standard of. qualilicatinn for those who arc permitted to assume our obligations.
cannot pass this question of .qualification of a member without
discussing for a moment the requirement of our laws that applicants
for the degrees must be able literally to conform to our work. It
seems to me that this is placing too much stress upon the physical
r~ther than the mental equipment of candidates. Tn makinQ," my visitatlons throl'ghout the state my attention has been repeatedly called to
men who are extremely dcsiron:; of becoming ~Tasons. men who are
eminently qualilied mentally and morally, and ):et who suffer from some
physical imperfection, g;enerally slight, that disqualifies them under
our laws. In every instance these men were enthnsiasticallv endorsed
hy the Masons in the localities in which they li,·c. Som~ arc men
whose ancestors for many generations have been zealons ~Tasons, and
who by reason of this association felt keenly the misfortune that precluded .them from following in their footsteps. I feel that this great
frate.rmty ~ould he taking a long step in the .right direction if the
reqmrement as to physical, qualification were eliminated from our laws
and the whole matter left. to the wise discretion of_ the local lodges, 0 :
at least that the law be amended so as to require only substantial physical confor.mity, leaving a very large discretion in the subordinate lodge
to determme what shall constitute "substantial" conformity. In other
words, where the local lodge shall favorably pass upon the physical

There is a pronounced tendency of the Grand Lodge, acting within
its undoubted constitutional authority, to curtail the independent activities of the constituent lodges. Wherever it is practicable, I am disposed to think that we should extend the field of activity in the local
lodge, grant them a wider discretion and impose upon them greater
respons'.bilities. I think this would result in the development of a
higher standard of citizenship within our order. Those of us who
are familiar with the character of the discussions in Masonic lodges
know that questions are seldom debated along broad lines of Masonic
policy. The right or justice or equity of the subject matter is relegated
to the background, and the issue to be determined usually finds expression in the question, "Have we a right to do it? Is not this a question solely under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge?" We should
be more liberal with the constituent lodges. \Ve should foster the
development of the individual Mason in his local surroundings, rather
than to make him feel that he is a mere automaton expressing the
will of a sovereign power on all questions affecting his well-being.

NECROLOGY.

I had beeu in hopes that I might repeat with all the sincere gratifi

cation it would afford the report of the Past Grand :V1aster Monroe,
wherein he said: "\Ve thank the Great Architect of the universe that
the cycle of time has not cnt down any officer of this Grand Lodge
since our last Communication."
The silent scepter of death has removed out of the great East
one of the great lights of Masonry in this Grand Jurisdiction. On the
14th day of January, 1914, Past Grand Master Foshay, while actively
performing the duties as chief executive of one of the great fraternal
organizations of this state, was stricken in death, and thus was smitten
one of the great pillars of Masonry in California. Little did we think,
my brethren, that this great, active man. strong mentally and physically, as he thrilled us with his wonderful voice in the opening of the
first Communication of this Grand Lodge in this magnificent Temple,
would not be able within a few short months to respond again to roll
call. Past Grand Master Foshay was a genuinely lbvable characterhonest, fearless, able. He has left an indelible influence OJ\ Masonry,
as well as the citizenship of this state. It may be well said of him, as
was said of one of his predecessors, "No, not dead, but gone beforegone to the reward which a busy and useful life, spent not for self

ll

A few months after the closing of the last session of the Grand
Lodge, and on the 17th day of .:\farch, 1914, the venerable Grand Bible
Bearer, Edwin A. Sherman, weighted down with years and honors,
passed peacefully to the Great Beyond. He was a conscientious,
earnest, faithful, active citizen, a Mason long before a large majority
of us who are here assembled appeared upon the scenes of this world's
activities. Major Sherman loved Masonry and never lost sight of a11
opportunity of singing its praises. It was the guiding star of his
destiny.
"Their voices are silent, yet they speak to us;
Their forms are unseen, yet they are with us."
Shortly after the death of Brother Sherman, I appointed John P.
Jarman of San Jose Grand Bible Bearer to succeed Brother Sherman.

'.

The death roll in other Grand Jurisdictions is a long one and
contains the names of men not only prominent in ~1asonrv in their
several states, but also men who have stood foremost in . state and
national life. vVe particularly note the passing of the late United States
Senator, Henry M. Teller, Past Grand Master of Colorado, a man of
wonderful activity, splendid ability and unswerving fidelity to every
trust.

the good fortune to attend the public installation of the officers of
Sequoia Lodge. At both of these meetings there was a large attend;ince and the greatest enthusiasm was manifested.
On November 6th I e::invened the Grand Lodge of California in
University Lodge No. 394 at the city of Los Angeles and laid the
corner-stone of the new National Guard Armory in that city. On this
occasion a patriotic address was delivered by General Frank C. Prescott, and the Grand Lodge was honored by an escort of Knight Templar. There was an enthusiastic assemblage of patriotic citizens and
Masons to witness the ceremony.
On November 22d I paid an official visit to Charter Rock Lodge
No. 410 of Berkeley and found this youngest of the representatives of
the brotherhood in the l.~niversity City to be in flourishing condition
and enthusiastic workers in the cause.
On November 24th I was invited by the members of the. Acacia
Fraternity of Berkeley to be their guest at dinner and for the evening.
I was much impressed with the earnest and conscientious demeanor of
the thirty or more young Masons whom I found to constitute the membership of this fraternity, and I could readily appreciate th" power
for good that they must exercise in the university community. Many of
these young men by their own efforts were supporting themselves
through their university course. They are under heavy· expense for
rentals, and it occurred to me that some benevolently disposed Masons
who possess the means to justify it could find no more laudable object
for their bo11ntv than to erect, equip and transfer to these worthy young
Masons and tl~cir successcrs a suitable place of shelter. At Stanford

I. I am asked whether property should be deeded to the trustees
of the lodge or to the Master or to the lodge directly. As this is an
important question, and one about which there has been considerable
confusion, I take the liberty of quoting in full the present statute of
the State of California on the subject, Statutes 1911, page 572.
"All unincorporated benevolent or fraternal societies or
associations are, and every lodge or branch of such society or
association is, hereby at•thorizcd and empowered without incorporation to purchase, receive, own, held, mortgage, manage and
sell, all such real estate and other property as may be necessary
for the business, purposes and objects of said society, association, or lodge. or branch; subject to the laws and 1·egulations
of said society or association, or lodge or branch, and of the
Grand Lodge thereof; and also to take and receive by will or
deed,. all property, not so necessary, and to hold the same until disposed of within a period of ten years from the acquisition thereof; provic!ed, that all conveyances transferring or in
anywise affecting the title to real estate owned or held by
such society or asscciation shall be executed by the presiding
officer and recording secretary under its seal. after a resolution duly adopted hy said society or association authorizing
the same."
This does away with the necessity for conveying to trustees and
the corresponding difficulty of keeping track of their st·ccessors, and
is such a sane and simple manner of conveying and recetvmg property that it seems to me it should be generally followed by the craft.

or Stated '.\Ieetings of the Lodge. However, in this case the

To the end that there may be a uniformity in the status of all

3. Yolo Lodge No. 81 suspended Brother 'William Samuel \Vall,
upon a certified transcription of the trial record from Churchill Lodge
No. 26. located at Fallon, Xevada, and requested me to pass 11pon the
correctness of their action.
After a comiderable investigation of this subject I am enaUe to
discover in the Ma sonic J nrisprudencc of this Grand Jurisdiction where
the question here suggested has e\·cr been considered or determined.
It is a question of far-reaching importance and great concern not
only to the craft in this, lmt all other Grand Jurisdictions, and merits
serious reflection ancl definite and final determination. In the absence of precedent or affirmative legislation on the subject any con·
clusion I may reach will necessarily be largely suggestive and serve
merely to bring the matter to the attention of the Grand Lodge at its
next annual comnmnication for affirmative action.
V1/ c claim the right by constitutional enactment to regulate the
conduct of Masons residing or sojourning within our territorial jurisdiction, and in doing this we care not from whence they come or to
what jurisdiction they acknowledge allegiance. \Ve claim to exercise
the right to try them in the tribunals of the order for any Masonic
offense committed within our borders and to inflict such punishment
as is warranted by our laws. Of course, we do not contend that the
judgment of our tribunals have any binding force beyond the territorial limits of our Grand J urisdictio11. ·while this is true. in my
judgment, it would be a long step in the right direction if each Grand
Jursdiction claiming this right would incorporate in its fundamental
law affirmative enactment making immediately effective the conviction
of any of its non-resident membership in other jurisdictions; reserving, however, the right to finally adjudicate the matter so far as it
affects the permanent statns of the accnsed in this jurisdiction by procuring a transcription of the trial record from the foreign jurisdiction,
and letting it take tlw ;;ame course as is now prescribed for trial
records in our own jurisdiction.
ln uthcr \\'Ords, that we recognize as imnJ<:diatcly diccti\·e the
j11dgment pronounced in a foreign jurisdiction as determinative of th.:
slatus of the accnsctl until the next succeeding annnal commLmic;ition
of our own Grand Lodge, when final adjudication cif the status of the

At the same time and in this same connection the Grand Lodge
should outline a procedure for the restoration to the rights and privileges of Masonry, all Masons convicted of Masonic offense in foreign
jurisdictions.

In the case at bar I find no warrant in law for the action taken
by Yolo Lodge :t\' o. 81, in entering the judgment of conviction against
\Villiam Samuel \Vall, a member of that Lodge, upon the certified
record of his conviction in Churchill Lodge No. 26, of the State of
>l"evada, and the action of the Lodge in that respect is therefore disapproved.
4. The Master of a Lodge should not permit any member to enter
or retire after announcing the report of the committee and directing
the ballot, unless sickness or some other imperative reason should
he pleaded. It is clearly within the province of a Master to prevent
brethren from evading the plain provisions of the law by retiring to
the anteroom for that purpose. If the 'Master has reason to question
the ~ood faith of members retiring to the Tylers' room preceding or
pcndmg a ballot, he certainly would be acting within his discretionarv
powers in directing and compelling them to return to the lodgeroot;1
and j)articipate in the ballot. I do not believe it incumbent upon the
Master to inquire as to whether brothers are in the anteroom prior
to ordering a ballot, but he has no power to excuse a member from
voting who asks it, whether in the lodgeroom or in the anteroom.

6. The question is asked whether it is proper for a person not
a member of the Lodge to see its hooks, and whether the practice of
permitting Lodge books to be audited by a member of the fraternity
other than a member of the Lodge is justified under our law.

procedure of the Master in the matter was correct in literally following the Constitution, Part 4, Article l, Section 1.

It does not seem to me that there is anything to construe in that
section; the language is perfectly clear, and if the count made by your
Secretary is correct. and for the purpose of this judgment it must be
assumed to be correct, your ruling of the Master that it required a
majority vote of the members present to elect is manifestly correct.
In this connection it might be well to say that in making a count the
Master ought to take into consideration Section 3, Part 4, Article 1,
in determining the question as to what memhers are entitled to vote.
That section reading, "None but members in good standing whose
dues are paid shall be entitled to vote at an election."

So far as I have been able to investigate the matter, I am of the
opinion that it was not the intention of the Grand Lodge in disposing
of the matter referred to in Section 150 (K) of the Constitution, to
hole! that it was a ::\1asonic offense to permit a Master :\fason to ins1wct the books of a Lodge other than the one to which he belongs.
I am satisfied that the word "personal," ·as used in that section, means
:;ome person other than a }faster Mason. Of course, the record iu
the case referred to was destroyed in the great fire of 1906, and we
are unable to ascertain just what the nature of the charges were against
the Secretary referred to in that section, but must assume that W did
not refer to a Master Mason.

I conclude, that, taking these two sections together. it requires a
majority vote of the members present, who are entitled to vote, to
determine an election. To hold a11y other way would be to read
something into the Constitution that is not there at present. Where the
language is plain I see no reason for attempting any forced construction.

Y 011 would be committing no Masonic offense in ha Ying your
books inspected by a l\Iastcr l\Iason in good stanuing other than a
member of your Lodge.

9.
can see no objection to the Secretary of the Lodge donating
for social or charitable purposes, as he sees fit, such amount as the
Lodge allows him as compensation for his services as Secretary.

7.

Section 488 of Anderson's Manual provides:
"There is nothing unmasonic, or even reprehensible, in
holding a dancing party in a Masonic hall. Social festivities,
when properly conducted, do not desecrate the lodgeroom, it
being understood, of course, that members on such occasions
are not to be clothed as Masons."

1 take it that the same condition would prcyail with relation to
social card games, where no Yiolation of the state or municipal laws
is involved. It is a matter that is and should be left largely to the
wise discretion of the particular Lodge. And in the event that objection thereto should reach such proportions as to cause serious dissension in the Lodge, great care should be exercised in passing upon
the matter.

Where it j:; apparent that there are members who are seriously
and conscientiously opposed to these pastimes taking place in the lodgeroom, their objections should be seriously considered, to the end that
the harmony of the Lodge and the best interests of the fraternity may
not be sacrificed.

ENDOWMl(NT FUND AND MASONIC HO:\!ES

1 feel a vital and continuing interest in the success of our Endowment Fund project. There is a well-defined sentiment, amounting
almost to a conviction, that properly and intelligently directed effort
will result in interesting well-to-do Masons in this jurisdiction in the
founding of a permanent endowment fund for the maintenance of the
Masonic Homes at Decoto and San Gabriel. It is our desire to es-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

27

tablish a million dollar fund, the interest on the investment of which
alone is to be used for the maintenance of om Homes.
This plan was formally put in operation about four years ago.
and a large committee was appointed to spread the gospel of endowment and swell the funds to the desired proportions. As to the ability
and Masonic devotion of this committee there can he no question;
·nevertheless, the result of their labors have not been as encouraging
as the optimism of the committee anticipated, if we may judge of their
attitude from the concluding sentence to be found in their first report
to the Grand Lodge, wherein they say: HOne million dollars will do
this, and with the present membersh;p of approximately fifty thousand,
the raising of the desired sum ought to be a work of love and occupy
no greatly extended time."
Several thousand dollars in cash have been actually added to the
nucleus fund of thirty thousand dollars in existence when the committee was appointed. This, howewr, is not evidence that the work
of the committee has been entirely unavailing. It is well known that
·even the very small amount of publicity given to the movement has
produced beneficial results. Reports have been received from various
parts of the state .that indicate that the Homes are being remembered
by Masons in testamentary disposition of their property.
This is exactly the fruition contemplated by the originators of the
plan, although we opine that such purpose was not generally understood by the craft. It could not be reasonably expected that such
a fund could be accumulated in a day, a year, or a generation, nor
was it to be hoped that cash donations effective immediately would
form any considerable portion of the fund. If the plan is to succeed
it inust be given intelligent publicity. \Ve must educate the membership of this Grand Jurisdiction, not only as to the needs but also
as to the character of our Homes. Any ::\fason who will take the
opportunity to investigate will find onr California Homes second to
none in existence.
It has been our pleasure to visit the Homes repeatedly. and never
have we visited San Gabriel and looked into the happy, cheerful and
contented faces of the sixty inmates, without feeling that if there were
no other excuse for the perpetuation of this great fraternity, its contiimed existence is amply justified by the splendid results there exemplified. In the atmosphere of that institution one cannot but feel
the ihSpiration of the fruition of the noble purposes and the presence
of a gratified and protecting Divinity. And it is a significant fact
that the children who have gone forth into the world from the institution have universally made good and reflected credit on the parent
institution. And the work done at the Home at Decoto is equally as
important, equally as imperative from the standpoint of duty and re-

compelling force.
The educational propaganda in furtherance of this Endowment
Fund should be so thorough and effective that no well-to-do Mason
in this jurisdiction should he unmindful of the hopes and aspirations
of the Fraternitv in this respect to the end that, when the time shall
come for him t~ make final disposition of his worldly effects he must

SALJ\M FIR!\
Immediately upon learning of the disastrous fire at Salem, Mass.,
I directed the Grand Secretary to forward the following message to
the Grand Master :
"Melvin M. Johnson,
Grand Master of Masons,
Boston, Mass.
"Our Grand Master, John D. Murphey, extends his sympathy to the sufferers at Salem, and wishes to know if the
Grand Lodge of California can be of any monetary assistance in helping to alleviate their distress. If so, command us."
To which the following reply was received:
"Boston, July 8, 1914.

"Mr. Harry S. Johnson,
Asst. Grand Secy. of California,
San Francisco, Cal.
"DEAR SIR AND BRO.: On behalf of Grand Master Johnson, who is absent from the city during most of the current
month, I desire to return thanks for the kindly offer of assistance from your Grand Lodge. The Masonic Apartments at
Salem were not touched by the fire, and while in all some
eighty members of the Craft met with loss in a greater or less
degree, there appears to be no suffering among them that we
are not able to relieve ourselves, and we are, therefore, with
all due appreciation of the good wishes of those in other jurisdictions, proposing to take care of our own without calling for
their help.
"Please rest assured that in case of necessity we should
accept freely what is so freely offered, and should respond to
the needs of others in their distress just as heartily as if we
did not receive at the present time assistance from our brethren
outside of Massachusetts.
"Please see that our thanks are properly rendered to your
Grand Master.
THOMAS w. DAVIS,
"Yours fraternally,
Recording Grand Secretary."

THE MASONJC EMPLOYMENT BUREAUS.

The Masonic Employment Bl1reaus of Oakland, Los Angeles and
San Francisco are doing splendid work and deserve the encouragement of the fraternity, employment for several hundred men having
been procured l;y means of these bureaus both in San Francisco and
Los Angeles.
The vitalizing work which they have accomplished anti are performing in behalf of those whom misfortune and misadventure have
made the objects of our bene,·olcnt consideration should be brought
home to the Masons in this jurisdiction in such a way _that its importance will be understood and appreciated. The relief extended in
this jurisdiction through the regular channels provided by the great
Fraternity to which we arc proud to acknowledge allegiance is shared
by people representing enry civilized nation on earth. We care for
deserving l\Iasons and those dependent t:pon them, regardless of creed
or nationality. and without imposing any conditions as to reimbursement. This has not invariably resulted in good. Tt has resulted in
temporarily relieving distress, hut too often at the fearful cost of
breeding chronic idleness and impoverishing vital forces. It has been
forcibly impressed upon us that our charities have been too frequently
bestowed upon those whose only claim to our generosity has Leen
found in their ability to impose upon us hy misrepresentation.
We have encouraged dependency by indiscreet giving, and this
for the reason that no other method of alleviating distress had been
inaugerated. It was at this point that your splendid organization
stepped in and proposed a solution that was at once sane and saving.
It saves not only money, but, what is immeasurably more important,
it saves men by enabling them to maintain their self-respect and manhood, by affording them an opportunity through their own efforts to
provide for themselves, thus substituting independence for dependrnce.
There is nothing more humiliating to a man than to know that
he is dependent upon the benevolence of others. and there is nothing
more demoralizing to a spineless man than the knowledge that in
times of adversity he is certain of adequate provision for his maintenance. Security from want. by means of the activities of others, always breeds indifference. On the other hand there is nothing more
exalting than the consciousness that under the most desperate circumstances one has been able to work out his own salvation,
The efforts of these bodies to establish a medil1m through which
able-bodied Masons mav be enabled to overcome adversity without
asking charity are entitl~d to the encouragement and enthusiastic support of all right-thinking men, and particularly of all Masons, who
arc employers of labor in any of its branches.

33

It is the imperative duty of brethren in this jurisdiction to mm1mize the labors of these bodies in every way possible. Masons owe
it to them, owe it to themselves, and owe it' to the institution to help
them to help the distressed in this jurisdiction, and any failure of
loyalty in this respect is a failure to conscientiously perform the obligations they have assumed in the Order.
Let us hope that they will be able to broaden the scope of their
activities to such an extent that whenever a worthy, able-bodied Mason shall apply for assistance, he will Le given an operative implement and afforded an opportunity to use it.

TE~IPL£

ASSOCL\'flO:-;f

It is incumbent upon this Grand Lodgc, in conjunction with other
:\Iasonic bodies who are purchasers and owners of stock in the Masonic Temple Association, to devise some means of liquidating the
outstanding indebtedness. At the present time the entire income of
the property is not sufficient to pay the interest on the outstanding
obligations amounting to approximately $300,000, together with the
running expenses of the Temple. Stockholders of the Association,
Masons and Masonic bodies, have invested more than $700,000, from
which they receive no returns whatever. On the contrary, they arc
compelled to make good the difference caused by the failure of the
rentals to pay interest and running expenses.
By taking up the remaining less than one-third of the stock and
liquidating the indebtedness. the stockholders would immediately receive a return of 1Yz per cent on their whole investment, or an income of 4.Yz per cent on the amount necessary to raise in order to
cancel the indebtedness.
The faith of this Grand Lodge is pledged to the ultimate extingl1ishment of this indebtedness, and this it must do.
It requires no argument to show that ultimately this money must
come from the membership at large, by means of assessments on the
constituent lodges, unless the lodges themselves become the purchasers
in their own right. If the Grand Lodge takes up all of this remaining stock with funds supplied by the subordinate lodges, the entire
returns from rentals will go into the treasury of the Grand Lodge.
On the other hand, if the Masons and Masonic bodies' stockholders in
the Association, and the Lodges that have not yet subscribed for stock,
will take up this stock, they themselves will be the beneficiaries of
future returns. As the Lodges must ultimately pay this money, it
seems to me that it would be the wise thing to subscribe directly for
the stock rather than be compelled ultimately to pay for it through

34

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

assessments, and thus automatically cover the amount of all returns
into the treasury of the Grand Lodge as its assets.
I have great faith that the no distant future will find the entir~
rental space of this building producing revenue. The buildings actually in course of construction in the immediate vicinity, the completion of the }fonicipal Railway on Van ::\ ess Avenue, are hopeful signs
in this direction. 'vVlwn the entire building is rented, its revenues will
immediatelv make the invcstmeut a 4 per cent proposition. \Vhy should
the stockh~lders, owners of more than two-thirds of this great investment, permit the entire income to go to persons who have advanced
Jess than one-third of the money expended in the erection and furnishing of the Temple? Tt seems to me that it is unwise and indefensible as a financfr,l policy.
Aside from the business aspect, I think that as a matter of sentiment every Lodge in California should own some stock in the Temple
Association. The Temple wao erected to reflect credit on this great
fraternal organization, and it fully lives up to that purpose. There is
no Lodge in this state that would have sanctioned erecting anything
less imposing and inspiring-a credit to the fraternity and an ornament to the city, and the very Lodges that now refuse to subscribe
for any of the stock would have been the first to denounce a discreditable structure.
I sincerely trust that some means may be devised for the solution
of this important question in such a way that outsiders may not continue to enjoy all the revenues of the Temple for generations to come,
and whereby the owners of more than two-thirds of the stock in this
enterprise may be enabled to net some return for their investment,
however small that may be.
FUNl'.RALS

A matter of serious concern to I\fasons, particularly those in large
cities. is the time unnecessarily lost in attending funerals of deceased
brothers. The present method requiring Lodges to be formally opened
before attending a Masonic funeral consumes much time and entails
a great amount of inconvenience. It seems to me that the practice now
in'· vogue in some Eastern jurisdictions of permitting the Master to
call his Lodge members together at the place designated for the funeral,
there put on the proper
and conduct the funeral,
without the necessity of a formal
of the Lodge, would be a
wise solution of this question: and I recommend that the laws be
amended in such a manner as to permit the inauguration of this practice in this Grand Jurisdiction.

Jn response to many suggestions that the :\lasonic bodies of California should erect a lmilding and
for its maintenance on the

hut after a great deal oi correspondence back and forth, no tangible
results were accomplished and the entire matter was dropped.

NA'tlONAL GRAND LODGE OF FRANCE

It was with nrnch pleasure we were advised some time since of
the organization of a new Masonic body in France, known as The
National Grand Lodge of France, which organization was perfected
largely through the good offices and efforts of the Grand Lodge of
England. This newly-organized body complies strictly with our views
of ,vhat constitutes Masonry. It requires that the holy Bible shall
always be open upon the altar when the Lodge is open; that the Lodge
shall alwavs be opened and closed with an invocation to the Great
Architect ~f the lJniverse; that no religious or political discussions
will be permitted in the Lodge; that the Lodge as such will not take
part in any political affair, but that every indivi<lual brother will preserve complete liberty of opinion and action; that only brethren who
are recognized as trnc hrcthrcn by the Grand Ledge of England will
be received in Lodge.
I recommend that the Independent National Grand Lodge of France
he formally recognh:ed.

To the Jt:. rv:. G1wul Lodge of
Bowing in hmnhlc submission to the decree of the gre-at God in
whose hands arc all our destinies, and with grateful thanks to !he many
brethren and friends whose expressions of sympathy and hope buoyed
me in the dark hours when the wife who had been my companion from
tl1e days of my youth-my chum and adviser-was called to the Great
Beyond. I present my annual report with some apology for having been

Lodge appreciate the difficulties under which the husiness ot the year
has been
and I can say with the Psalmist. "Surely goodness and

THE LIRRARY,

. \Ve have many books, but mainly proceedings of other J urisdictlons. Of miscellaneous reading our library is sadly deficient. All the
books have been placed in modern cases and labeled and a card catalogue completed. A few donations have hccn made, but most of the
books are from the \V. Frank Pierce collection. :\ book-plate has been
adopted for those. the following being a copy:

OF THE

Grand Lodge of California
CASE........... ..

No ...........

In some of the Eastern Jurisdictions brethren who are interested
have presented to Masonic libraries collections on particular subjects,
and they are appropriately called "Memorial Collections." For instance, the late James D. Richardson filled one alcove in the library of
the Scottish Rite at Washington with books relating alone to the
politics, history and the public men of the 'Cnited States; Martin Collins contributed money to the amount of $1,300, which was expended
on books of travel and descriptions in the United' States and its possessions; William Busby of Oklahoma contributed $1,880 for a collection comprising science in general, mathematics, physics, astronomy,
electricity, mechanics, geology, ethnology, botany and natural history.
We have ample room in the Temple for any donations that may be
made.
Contributions have been made during the year as follows:
A picture of Jonathan D. Stevenson, our first Grand Master, by
Jas. F. Robinson, Grand Secretary of Oregon;
A part of the old. Temple at Post and Montgomery streets, being
the figure of clasped hands that ornamented the Post street entrance,
by Hermann Muller Hoadley of ~fount Moriah Lodge N'o. 44. So far
as we know, this is the only relic of the old Temple extant;
Photograph of old Temple, by George Bell of San Francisco Lodge

No. 360;

The cost of maintenance of the building for the past year is probably in excess of what it will be in the future because some extraordinary expenses incident to a first year's business have been necesEarily
incurred that will not occur again.
The building contains six meeting halls, rented as follows:
Commandery Hall-One regular tenant.
Blue Lodge Hall No. I-Rented 4 tenants.
Blue Lodge Hall No. 2-Rente<l 5 tenants.
Blue Lodge Hall No. 3-Rented 4 te11ants.
Chapter R. A. M. Hall No. 4-Rented 6 tenants.

These bodies now occupying these halls are paying rentals of from
30 to 40 per cent more than they paid to the old Temple Association,
and this, together with the fact that twenty-six Masonic bodies now
occupy space in the ))11ilding, clearly indicates the loyal support of the
San Francisco :\iasoas to the Fraternity in general and their pride in
the Temple.

increasing the per capita tax on its Subordinate Lodges, and to the
end that the Grand Lodge as well as all the stockholders may derive the
benefit of an income at the earliest moment we suggest that the Grand
Lodge provide for the retirement of the indebtedness by pledging itself
to subscribe and pay for stock to the amount of $25,000.00 annually
until the amount is liquidated. We feel assured that this tax on the
Grand Lodge will not continue many years, because the business of the
building will soon commence to be sufficiently profitable to materially
assist in the reduction of the debt.
WM. H. CROCKER,
President Masonic Temple Association of California.

64

The several offices on the top floor arc rented to the Grand Lodge,
the Grand Commandery, Chapter and Council, the Board of Relief, Em-

ployment Bureau and California Lodge, Chapter and Council.
The total rentals for halls and stores amount to about $2,000.00
per month.
Thus far the stores and other space on the ground floor of the
building have not rented, but the rapid encroachment of business
toward Van Ness Avenue and Market Street as a center gives abundant
assurance that the time is not far distant when this part of the building
will bring constantly increasing revenue. The close proximity to the
Civic
the new Municip<tl Street Railroad on Van Ness Avenue,
the opening of the Twin Peaks Tunnel, thereby connecting a large and
rapidly growing residence section with the l\farket Street district, give
promise of early business activity in the vicinity of our building.
At present the most serious problem confronting the Board of
Directors is the reduction of the large indebtedness of over $300,000.00
and its interest cost, which is our hea\•iest burden of expense. The
i\fasonic bodies of San Francisco, with an investment of $241,550.00,
have been generous in their subscriptions to stock, and have purchased
to the extent of their financial ability, and confidence in the ultimate
financial success of the building was further evidenced during the past
year by subscriptions for stock of over $6,000.00 from the Lodges and
individuals.
Many other Masonic bodies as well as brother Masons have also
indicated their pride and interest in the Masonic Temple of our great
State by generorndy subscribing to stock, and they will continue to do
so from time to time, but the burden is heaviest NOvV, and we feel
obliged to ask the assistance of the Grand Lodge to the extent of its
financial ability.
The spkndid bnilding is the :'.\JASO?\IC TEMPLE of our State,
and from loyalty to our great Order it commands the fraternal interest
of every Masonic body and of every Master Mason within our borders.
The Grand Lodge has. for the past few years, annually subscribed to
stock to the amount of from ten to fifteen thousand dollars, without

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

During the year ending August 31st, 1914, the following 75 Masons
or members of their families have passed to their final reward, and their
remains have been given burial with Masonic honors, or shipped according to the wishes of the families, viz. :

The Masonic Board of Relief. of the City of Los Angeles, herewith
presents the following report of its labors from September 1, 1913, to
,\ugust 31, 1914:
OFFICERS.
President .................................................................. Brother JOHN HlLL BEAN
Vice-President ........................................................ Brother DANA RErn \;VELLER

We have no apology to offer for the work of our Board during the
past year.
\Ve have done our duty as we saw it. \Ve believe that,all worthy
calls have been answered, and in several instances the broad plain of
l-l umanitv has been iiwadcd and the mantle of Charity has been extended t~ the widow and her children whose lack of Masonic standing
has been forfeited through no fault of theirs.
The 1111fortnnate condition existing in ::\Iexico has sent many people
into our midst in destitute condition who were in affluence before war
began in their republic.
There has been an unusual number of unworthy individuals applying for aid, and it has taken the greatest of care to avoid imposition. and
it has been our sorrow that we have felt it our duty to place several
men in custody, because of their dishonest practices.
IN\' AL IDS.

Brethren: This is no place for a really sick man, unless he has
plenty of means and is willing to part with his money. He can't live
on climate alone, and before any of the corporations will employ him
he must pass a severe physical examination. The examining physician
docs his work thoroughly and gives the corporation the benefit of the
doubt. A man over forty years of age has very little show for any
position.
Our l\fasonic Employment Durcau is doing a great work. The
manager reports the number of applications during the year.
Applications: l\Ten, 1118; womrn, 242; total, 1360.
Positions fillcll: l\fcn, 657; women, 106; total, 763.
The above represents good positions secured, lmt docs not include
minor nr temporary jobs of a few hours to a few days duration, of
which latter there were 1908.

SAN DIEGO BOARD OF RELIEF.

To the Jfost Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The l\fasonic Board of Relief of San Diego herewith presents a
report of its work cowring the period from September 1, 1913, to
August 31, 1914, inclusive.
The past year has Leen the most active in the history of this Board,
the number of cases handled and the amount of money spent for the
relief of sojourning brethren, their widows and orphans, far exceeding
that of any prC1·io11s year.
The percentage of refunds from IOllges primarily responsible for
cases handled this year has been good, and the Secretary, by systematic correspondence, was able to straighten out several old accounts,
some of which had run for two or three years.
We do not as yet maintain a regular Employment Bureau, but the
Secretary has been successful in placing quite a number of men and
women in positions. 11oth permanent am! temporary.
During the past year our Board has consisted of four lodges,
namely: San Dic?o :\ o. 35. :')ih·cr Cate Ko. 296, Blackmer, U. D., and
Coronado, U. D. The officers are Eclgar B. Levi, President; Arthur
A. Mathewson. Vice Presiclent; .'\. n. Haxton, Secretary, and John F.
Covert, Treasurer.
The following twenty-one brethren have been buried under the
auspices of this Bo;1rd, or their remains shipped according to wishes of
relatives:

REPORT OF THE CO~BUTTEE OF THE STATE Ol~
THE WAR IN ECROPE AND THE RELIEF OF
THE BRETHREX WHO ARE THEREIX
ENGAGED.
Brother Otto L. Sues from the Special Committee
heretofore appointed by the Grand Master to formulate a
report relative to our duty in the matter of relief to the
sufferers in Europe on account of the devastating war
now being ·waged, reported as follov.:s:
To the ~;i:t:. rv:. Gra11d Lodge of California.
Your committee to whom has been referred the investigation and
consideration of affairs >.Tasonic in war torn Europe, and the relief
of the brethren and their families therein engaged, beg leave to submit
the following report:
Your committee met in pursuance with the call of the chairman
and thoroughly considered a comnmnicatioll from the Grand Lodge of
Masons of Oregon and a printed report from the Grand Lodge of
England, being the only accessible data on the subject, and while we
are convinced that, as stated in the address of the Grand Master to the
Grand Lodge, "This is a vital and imperative matter-a matter of tremendous magnitude-and the solution calls for serious and conscientious consideration," we do not believe that this is the time for us to
act.· This subject needs consideration from a calm, sensible and wellbalanced st;mdpoint, free from the hysteria incident to times of war,
and the rashness to assist without
where and how to apply
the proper ancl adequate relief. California has a world-wide reputation for its humanity, sympathy with the distressed and assistance with
substantial aid. The Masonic fraternity of this great State and jurisdiction will not be found wanting when the time eomcs to
aid in
this instance, but we do not believe that that time has come.
\Ve
leave to here quote the time-worn adage: "Charity begins
at home." How many men in this grand jurisdiction, who are me111bers
of the Craft, have answered the call for the reservist and gone to the
front while their families remain here, possibly in need? We will not
have the answer until matters adj nst themselves and when the little
savings npon which existence is now dependent have hccn exhausted.
Even should we at this time make an appropriation of funds, to
whom and where conld they be sent? Even the Grand Lodge of England, much better informed on the subj cct than we can he expected to
be, makes its contribution to the English Red Cross fund and leaves

90

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the question of indh·idual relief to the various subordinate Lodges as
circumstances may ansc. Vv c, as :\Iasons, know no country, no sect,
no creed and no people, in assisting worthy Brother l\Iaster l\Iasons,
whithersoevcr dispersed around the globe, and it is impossible at this
time to get in touch with brethren of t,he various countries engaged
in war, "for in every country and in every clime arc l\fasons to be
found."
'vVe wish here to quote from the appeal of the President of the
United States for American neutrality: "A nation that neither sits in
judgment upon others nor is disturbed in her own counsels and which
keeps herself fit 'and free to do what is honest and distinterested and
truly serviceable for the peace of the world." So are we prepared to do
in the l\Iasonic fraternity of California, and for that purpose, and to that
encl, we believe the good judgment of the Grand l\lastcr, whoever he
may be, and the availability of the emergency fund of the Gram! Lodge,
to be fully adequate and sufficient.
Respectfully submitted,
CHAS.

There are now three hundred and sixty-seven Lodges, with a
total membership of fifty-three thousand one hundred and seventy-nine.
A number of new Temples have been dedicated during the year,
and many me re arc under construction, which shows the splendid financial condition cf the Lodges.
I have visited c\·ery district in the State, and in manv of the districts have visited every Lodge therein. I have held schools of instruction, both day ancl night sessions, ancl have given a great deal of private instruction to l\lasters, V/arclens, Deacons, Brethr<:n and Inspectors.

These schools have usually been well attended, the officers and
brethren manifesting an interest and keen desire to perfect themselves
in the ritual.
There are some Lodges in the mountain and other districts that
have a harcl struggle for existence, am! I fear will cventuallv have to
consolidate with some nearby Lodge, as their membership i~ so scattered they cannot get enough members together to hold meetings. This
condition is unfortunate, as many of these Lodges are \'cry old, and in
years past were good, strong Lodges; hut the industries in their communities have ceased and their membership has of necessity scattered
all over the universe.

The Grand Lecturer then presented the report of his
labors for the year as follows:

The inspectors of San Francisco and bay counties hav<e conferred
degrees at Santa Rosa, \Voodlancl, Fruitvale, San Jose and Mission
Lodge No. 169, San Francisco.

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:

These meetings have been attended by large numbers, and much
good accomplished, not only from the fraternal spirit of getting the
brethren together, but by the opportunity they have had of seeing the
work exemplified by the inspectors in a highly efficient manner.

Another year has passed and we again meet in annual session to
give an account of our stewardship for the year just closed.
At the outset we desire to offer up our most fervent prayers to the
ever-living Cod for the many blessings lie has bestowed upon us and
this great fraternity, and with grateful hearts we thank Him for the
peaceful prosperity that prevails in our country.
Never was Masonry in this jurisdiction more prosperous or the
Lodges in better condition numerically or financially.
The net gain the past year has been Twenty-nine H undrcd and
Twenty-two, the largest gain in the history of the Grand Lodge.
Thirteen new Lodges have received dispensations and several
more are now organizing.

I have had the pleasure of accompanying the :M:. w:. Grand
Master on many of his official visits throughout the State.
These visits create a great deal of interest among the Lodges.
The bret~r.en appreciate a visit from the Grand Master, many of the
Lodges v1s1tecl never before having thus been honored.

w:. Grand Lodge of California:

I hereby offer the following amendments to the Constitution:
That Section 82 be amended to read "seventy-five dollars" instead of
"fifty dollars," as it now reads. and by adding after the words "consent
of all" in the fifth line thereof the words "and none of them shall charge

That Section 150, sub. 8, be amended to read as follows : "To report to the Grand Secretary, immediately after their occurrence, all

their ages, nativity, business and residence."

The following resolution was unanimously adopted this afternoon:
"WHEREAS, At this the sixty-fifth Annual Communication of this
Grand Lodge, two members of this Grand Lodge, each of whom has
been honored by preferment herein, viz.: M. W. George Clement
Perkins, Past Grand Master, and Brother William Kettner, present
Grand Marshal, are absent in attendance upon the session of the Congress of the United States, and we are thereby deprived at this Communication of their wise and reassuring counsel and genial companionship ; and
WHERE.\S, The high and patriotic service of these honored brothers
in the highest legislative departments of our government is of such a
character as to not only contribute materially to the welfare of our
common country, but also to bring added honor to this Grand Bodv
because of their membership and office herein; now, therefore, be it •

Resolved, That the Grand Secretary be instructed in the name of
the Grand Lodge, to telegraph to Past Grand Master Perkins and
Grand Marshal Kettner the greetings of this Grand Lodge with the
assurance that though absent from our midst they and their services to
the country and to the craft are eyer in our minds, and that we bespeak for them a safe return to their homes, and the actiYe resumption
of their l\Iasonic affiliations with their brethren of California.

To the JJ.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee appointed for the purpose of formulating a rule
whereby our Lodges may be advised as to who should be admitted as
visitors, respectfully report that we find it very difficult to establish
a hard and fast rule except along general Masonic lines. That on
acc0t111t of the chaotic condition of Masonry in European Countries,
especially at the present time, and the deplorable lack of information
relative to l\lasonry in the Republics to the south of us, we deem it
inadvisable to make any report' at this Communication of the Crand

The Grand Secretary, at the request of a number of
brethren, presented a proposed amendment to Section 73
of the Constitution, which was referred to the Committee
on Jurisprudence. It is as follows:
73.

DISPENSATlO)J FOR-PREREQUISITES.

Upon the petition of twelve and not more than twenty-five, :'.\laster
Masons in good standing, accompanied by the <limits or ccrtiticates of the
signers in the forms prescribed in Sections 159 all(! 161, being presented to the Grand ;\faster, in the form prescribed in Section 235, he
may, in cases of manifest propriety and necessity grant them a dispensation to open and hold a Lodge at the place therein to be named,
under such name as shall be approved by him, which shall not be the
name of any living person or chartered Lodge, with power to make
Masons and receive members by affiliation; and he shall therein appoint the Master and \Vardens of the new Lodge. But in no case shall
such dispensati011 be issued unless the petition be accompanied by a
;ecommendation from the nearest or most convenient chartered Lodge,
1£ from a town or city where more than one Lodge exists, then from
a majority of such Loclgcs, setting forth, in the form prescribed in
Section 237, that the petitioners are all Master Masons in good standin~, that the establishment of the new lodge is of manifest propriety and
will conduce to the good of the order, and that a safe and suitable
Lodge room has been provided therefor; nor unless the petition shall
also be accompanied by a certificate from an Inspector whom the
Grand Master shall select, declaring that the Master and Wardens,
proposed in such petition are each fully competent properly to confer
the three degrees of Masonry and to deliver entire the lectures thereunto appertaining.

w:. Grand Lodge of California:

The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California
ht'rcwith submits for your consideration and approval its annual report for the year ending September 30th, 1914.
The ]\f. ·. \.V. ·. Grand Master re appointed Thomas Flint, vice
self. term expired, and the Board helcl its annual meeting at the
office of the Grand Secretary on October 18, 1913, re-elected \Vm. S.
Wells president, ;\fotlcy H. Flint, vice-president, and Elmer E.
Stone. secretary, and has during the year held its regular and special meetings at both Decoto and San Gabriel.
The reports of the secretary, superintendent and accountants are
herewith presented, made a part of this .report and referred to for
a more particular statement of the financial and general condition
of both Homes.
We fully reported in our last annual report as to the water
situation, and the year just passed has demonstrated that our supply
is entirely sufficient. The State Highway Commission is now building the State Highway from a point between Hayward and Niles
and in front of the Home property. This is a public work, and one
in which we are very much interested. The Commission itself is
doing the work, and it was necessary that they should obtain water
from us, as there was no other supply. We have permitted them
to put in a pipe and to take water from us not to exceed fifty thousand gallons a day while they are so engaged in this work, for which
they are to pay us 12 cents per hundred gallons. This charge will
more than cover the cost of the water and the pumping of it, and
the wear and tear on the machinery. They draw from the lower
reservoir, so it only requires the pumping from the well into that
and not the use of the two pumps. While we are not engaged in the
business of furnishing water to anyone, thi:; was a work of such nature and character that we deemed it for the hst interests of all to
assist so far as we were ahk, and if we did not it would
the
work until another year.
The vineyard has been a source of expense to ns for some years.
The vi11<'s arc dying and the two dry seasons have about ended their
usefulness. \Ve dug up about a third of the vineyard last year and
added the ground to our hay crop. \Ve shall take up this year all of
the balance of the vineyard planted to wine grapes and only retain
such part of it as is planted to table grapes and of that only sufficient
to supply the Home. The cultivation of this vineyard has for year;;
been a severe tax on the resources of the Home and the raising of
hay upon this land will net us far more than the returns yearly received from the vineyard.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

101

\Ve have moved the six cottages back beyond the Simonoff Temple and have cleared and graded the strip of land between tht Temple
and the kitchen, and have let the contract for a new dormitory building to contain fifty-two rooms. The present kitchen is in a very bad
condition and requires overhauling and remodeling. We have planned
a new kitchen to be added on to our present kitchen, enlarging the
dining room to fulfill future demands. These improvements are absolutely necessary in view of the fact that every room is now occupied and we have between fifteen and twenty applications under consideration, but which cannot be acted upon until we have room. The
new dormitory bllilding when completed and fully furnished, together
with the work on the kitchen, will cost in the neighborhood of $50,000.
and in order to pay for this work it will be necessary to continue the
50 cents per capita tax for the ensuing year.
\Ve have also adopted a general plan of improvements and have
had a drawing of the same made and will submit it to yon for your
inspection, one showing the present buildings as they are now located,
together with the new dormitory building and a proposed dormitory
building to the west of the present administration building; another
showing wings added to the administration building, both of which will
constitute the future improvements at the Home. These can be built
one at a time as required, and when completed will take care of the
needs of the Home for many years to come.
We have removed the fifteen thousand gallon oil tank which was
located at the Home to the depot at Dccoto, and have leased from the
Southern Pacific Railroad Company a piece of land and have there
placed it, together with a pump and plant, which will enable us to
handle our own oil supply instead of depending upon someone else.
This will give us a storage capacity at the Home and at the depot of
about thirty thousand gallons.
The Home at San Gabriel has maintained its usual condition as
far as the property and buildings are concerned, except by the damage
suffered through the excessive floods which prevailed all over Southern
California last winter. The stream, ordinarily twenty-five feet wide
when flowing its strongest. was caused to
its course and wash
a bed three times that width within three days, and also cat:sed practically a total loss of our garden stuffs, then planted. This has been
repaired by straightening the channel and constructing barriers on each
side of the wash, which repair and improvement cost approximately
$1,600, but leave us much better protected against future floods. This
condition, however, will he a continual menace to us. Our fruits and
berries are in the best of condition and the garden is now re-established and producing most satisfactorily. The ornamental portions of

the grounds, untler the master hand of Brother Bettes, presents the
most pleasing appearance in the history of the place. The tennis court
and playground, however, 'have not been restored to their former condition, as the expense necessary for permanent work is thought not

Your authorization of last year to dispose of the San Gabriel
property and buy other property, if in our judgment we deemed best,
has been caretulfy considered by your Board. We have investigated
many tracts in that vicinity, but as yet have found nothing that is
tlltisfactory, or that we deemed of importance enough to be considered,
and we still have the matter under consideration.
The result of the atmosphere maintained in this Home are manifested by the singular success of every boy leaving the Home the
past three or four years for the more useful fie.Ids of life. Their training and instruction have proven them well fitted to meet their new
conditions, and well fortified with the courage and integrity necessary
to succeed in their undertakings. We are proud that they conduct
themselves after leaving the Home so as to reflect honor 'on the institution. We are giving to the world strong, keen, honest, industrious young men, who, were it not for the timely and thoughtful care
of this great fraternity might have drifted into very uncertain channels. We ,cannot lciok at these boys and young men without feeling
a pride that we shared in shaping their lives for useful and honorable
careers. Our girls, too, are exceptionably proficient in all · their attainments, and many display a gifted talent in musical or other artistic
lines. The generous and interested business men of our fraternity
are liberal in the development of our boys in their several lines, because their active efforts bring almost immediate returns. Those,
ltowever, interested in the development of a sweet voice, or a course in
art for our girls are less numerous, and we sometimes witness one of our
talented musicians take up a course in stenography or some more
prosaic vocation when we believe the world has been deprived of something of value in their nature, or probably some sweet song that would
give joy to thousands; is 11tilled at its very source.
A beloved and prominent member of the Grand Lodge of California, who i:equests that his name be withheld, has arranged with
your Board of Trustees, to provide a vocational scholarship each year
for some child of the Home after finishing their schooling. He is
as wise as he is good in providing a scholarship for the girl or boy
who, after securing all the training and care the Home can give, may
be lifted up in the world just as they are entering into it. What
period of our lives is more important or more critical than when we

Suitable entertainments and out-of-door recreations have been provided for the members of the Homes. by means of which the older
members have occupied their time with wholesome diversions, while
the younger members have been afforded that incentive and opportunity

DECOTO.
There are now at the Decoto Home 121 residents, 79 men and 42
women. During the year there have been admitted 17 men and 9 women.
All the rooms arc now occupied. Applications for admission have
been far in excess of the vacancies as they occur. The waiting list
is constantly growing, and the need for additional room is most urgent
to n'!eet the demands of the Lodges throughout the jurisdiction.

Each month arrangements are made so that the brethren and

Alameda Lodge, No. 167, F. & A. :VI., and Orient Chapter, No. 177,

All holidays have been observed in an appropriate way. Arbor
Day was added to the list this year. A program consisting of readings, recitations and songs was given, after which all gathered on the
grounds in front of the main building and a number of trees were
planted by the residents of the Home. The observance of this day
will also become an annual event. All of the gatherings mentioned
above are well attended.
Manv other entertainments have been given for the pleasure and
benefit ~f the family by Lodges, members of Lodges and their ladies.

contributed to our musical and literary programs.
During the Christmas holidays, two enjoyable events were had
worthy of mentio·n. A play was given, entitled "The Country School,"

Eve a carnival and watch party was held in the Assembly Hall, which
was attended by all the members of the family.

SAN GABRIEL.
The Orphans' Home at San Gabriel, like a bud unfolding into a
beautiful rose, is growing each year with added charms among the
children, better efficiency in music, dances, drills and special instruction, and the development of the older children blossoming out into
that interesting period, when the first view of the outside world is
pictured before them, and they anxiously aspire to choose an active,
useful and helpful vocation in life.
The policy of the Trustees in placing boys at the age of 14 or 15
in the hands of some responsible Mason, or firm under the direction
of a Mason, to learn a trade or business and at the same time complete their schooling, has met with unquestioned success. Similar
provision has been made with some of the girls. This policy has the
effect, however, of reducing the average age of the children very materially, as most new :;dmissions are small children. Their tender

GP.AND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

112

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

age makes them more easily adjusted to their new environment, and
growing with conditions in the Home facilitates discipline.
\Vhen the San Gabriel Home was opened five years ago, there
were 13 boys and 13 girls, of an average age of 12 years. Since that
time we have admitted 89 children. Fifty-four have been provided
for in vocations or returned to parents, and one lost by death, leaving
now in the Home 61 children, 34 boys and 27 girls, the average age
now being 10 years. During this period only three children have been
dismissed from the J.fome because of ineligibility, addiction of dangerous habits, or incorrigibility. All other children have responded well
to the care and discipline of the Home, and we watch with interest
the changing methods of the new child as it throws off the rough
ways acquired in less favorable surroundings, without a parent's care,
and adopts almost involuntarily the sweet mannerisms taught by their
thoughtful instructors.
The Home life, from a social point of view, is active, original and
such as to inspire a continuous interesting entertainment. Each Sun·
day evening a small number of the children provide a new program
for the remainder. The next week a different committee provides the
program; thus it is never tiring, and never old. All patriotic and
other holidays and anniversaries of importance are suitably observed,
and a paper read giving the origin and explanation of the observance
of the occasion. Many older persons could benefit much by these
papers.
The notable event of each year is the camping trip of the children.
This healthful and most pleasant diversion is of inestimable value to
the children. This year the camp was again at "Camp Collins" on
Balboa Island, in Orange County, so named because of the generous
action of W. S. Collins in giving the grounds, water, and many other
privileges, without cost, to the children. Boating, fishing. swimming,
launch rides, camp fires, and all the pleasures of camp life were
enjoyed. They lived in their tents this year from July 23d to Sep·
tember 3d. In the active management of the camp, those in charge
were treated as guests and the camp was operated by the "Camp
Collins Club." They chose their own President and Secretary, and
appointed committees for the active work of the camp, who performed
their services well. A paper of much merit and interest was published
every morning. Side trips to neighboring beaches were made, and a
contest in swimming with a neighboring camp, in which our boys excelled, provided much pleasure.
Our Health Board still remains almost perfect. No more capable,
generous, good-hearted, thoughtful and deserving man exists than Dr.
J. M. Dunsmoor, Secretary of the Board of Relief of Los Angeles.
He is at all times watchful of the health of the Home and children.

Past Crand ::\faster Frank J\T. .\ngcllotti, Chairman of the
Committee on Jurisprudence, reported as follows:
To the JI.'.

rv:. Gra11d J,odgc of Calilornia:

Your Committee on Jnrisprmknce have had under cnnsi(k•ration the
Yarious decisions rendned hy the Grand l\Iastcr dnring the year.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

129

There can be no question as to the correctness of the decisions of
the Grand .Master No. l, respectively 1-5-6-7-8-9-10.

In decision No. 2 the only point really decided by the Grand
Master was that in a case where the Master had issued a summons
requiring the attendance of members at a stated meeting of his lodge,
which summons had been duly served, and which some of the members had refused to obey, the summons having been issued and served,
it was not the province of the members so requested to appear to
question either the legality or the propriety of the issuance of the
summons. In this ruling the Grand Master was certainly correct. The
Grand ::\faster, however, stated that he was disposed to think that it
was not the intention of the .Masonic law that the suimnons should be
issued for the purpose of procuring attendance of members at either
special or stated meetings of the lodge. \Ve are of the opinion that
this is not a correct statement of the law in this jurisdiction. It has
been twice held by this Grand Lodge that the :\faster has power to
issue a summons whei1ever the business of the lodge requires it, and
the brother receiving it has no right to c1nestion its legality and refuse
to obey. (Vol. 4, Proceedings 353; Vol. 6, Procee<lings 1084.)
The latter of the decisions issued was a case where the ]\faster
had issued summons to the members of his lodge requiring them to
attend a special meeting for the purpose of conducting funeral services
of a deceased hrother. Of course it is not contemplated by law that
summons should he issued for attendance at ordinary meetings of the
lodge, but unquestionably. the Master has power to issue summons for
any meeting whenever he is of the opinion that the bl1siness of the
lodge demands such action on his part. Disobedience of such summons
is a Masonic offense for which an offending brother may be informed
against and tried.
With these modifications the decision of the Grand :'.\foster is
approved.
Decision 3 presents, as is stated by the Grand l\faster. a question
of far reaching importance and great concern, one that merits serious
reflection and final definite determination. Brother 'Wm. Samuel Viall
of our Yolo Lodge Ko. 81, residing in the jurisdiction of Churchill
Lodge No. 26, of Fallon, N' evada, was proceeded against in the latter
lodge for un-Masonic conduct, and by such lodge convicted and suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry. Churchill Lodge
thereupon certified the record of the proceedings to our Yolo Lodge
No. 81, which latter lodge with such record as its only hasis, without
any trial, entered a judgment of suspension against the brother.
The Grand Master decided that there was no warrant in law for
the action taken by our Yolo Lodge X o. 81, and therefore disapproved

130

PHOCEEDINGS OF '!'HE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the same. Jn this ruling we arc satisfied that the Grand .:\faster was
correct and his decision must he approved. If the judgment of the
Nevada Lodge ipso facto operated to deprive Brother Wall of his
in this state, no judgment of suspension was essential in our
Yolo Lodge; if it did not ha vc such an effect, he could not be deprived
of his standing in om ledge without a trial therein.
The seri0t's question presented by these facts is as to the effect of
the action of the :\'evada Lodge upon the status of Brother Wall as
a member of our Yolo Lodge. Did it ipso facto deprive him of his
c\Iasonic standing in this jurisdiction? \Ve think this question merits
iurther consideration than we are able to give it at this Communication
of the Grand Lodge. and we recommend that it be referred to our successors. The sanw
to be said as to the suggestion of the Grand
:\laster as to the desirability of
certain legislation relating
to the effect of judgments of foreign jurisdictions.
As to decision 4.
\Ve understand the decision of the Grand Master to be substantially as follows:
The Master of the lodge should not permit any member to retire
after announcing the report of the committee on investigation and
directing a ballot, unless sickness or some other imperative reason is
shown. It is clearly then the province of the }faster to prevent brethren
from evading plain provisions of the law by retiring to the ante-room
for that purpose. If a Master has a reason to question the good faith
of members retiring to the Tyler's room preceding or pending a ballot,
he certainly is acting within his discretionary power in requesting or
compelling them to return to the lodge room and participate in the
ballot. The Master has no power to excuse a member from voting
who asks it, whether in the lodge room or the ante-room.
\\' e think this correctly states the law and we recommend that the
decision of the Grand Master is approved.
Respectfully submitted,
F. 1vL ANGELLOTTI,
WM. F. WELLS,

REPORT OF COl'vI:\HT'I~EE ON GRAr\D LECTURER'S
REPORT.
Brother J. Stewart Ross. for the committee to whom
had been referred the annual report of the Grand Lecturer,
reported as follows, which was adopted:
To the ;w:. ~v:. Graiid Lodge of California:
Your Committee to whom w;;s referred the annu;;l report of the

V.'. vV. :. Thomas J. Baker, Grand Lecturer, has had the same under
consideration and begs leave to report as follows:
The report, which details the satisfactory condition of the lodges
throughout the state under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lecturer,
shows most emphatically the surpassing ability with which the Grand
Lecturer performs his ever increasing duties .
We feel that that portion of his report which shows that hr has
practically reached every nook and corner of this great jursidiction
and come in personal conduct with the :VIasons of each section, not
only shows his marked and zealous devotion to the duties of his office,
hut in a large way accounts for the unprecedented prosperity in our
lodges both numerically and financially, for though i\fasonry by no
means consists in mere efficiency of ritualistic work in the lodges,
nevertheless, the impressiveness and accuracy with which the lectures
are delivered by the i\Iasters and officers adds much to the benefits
which the candidate receives from the degrees and continues his interest
in the work which is the real secret of the prosperity of our lodges.
Your Committee especially invites your attention to that part of
Brother Baker's report in which he emphasizes the necessity for
extreme carefulness in the selection of candidates by the lodges and
to the further fact that he reports that the lodges are observing this
most important duty which further accounts for the prosperity' of our
order.
In conclusion, we desire to commend the entire report of the
Grand Lecturer not only for that part of the tmprecedented success
of the past year that may justly and properly he attributed to him,
hut for the courtesy and harmony that is shown throughout the report
to exist between onr very \Vorshipful Brother, Thomas J. Raker,
and all those with whom he has had communicatio11.
J. STEWART Ross,
