and four "not guilty." The Master received this vote as a verdict a111!
at the next meeting of the lodge announced the result, and, declaring
it to be in effect a verdict of acquittal, directed his Secretary to
enter judgment accordingly. From this an appeal was taken by the
?\faster of the Lodge of which the accused \Vas a member, the Junior
\Varden having preferred the charges, and the following questions
were before the Committee on Grievances in their consideration of
the appeal:

it is proper to note that while we are satisfied of the good faith
of the Commissioners and have no doubt that they acted conscientiously in the matter, we can not forbear saying that notwithstanding the apathy of the prosecution of which they complained, there
was sufficient evidence adduced to warrant a verdict of guilty if the
· Commissioners believed the testimony given by the witnesses who
were produced by the prosecution. On the other hand, if after having heard the testimony and observed the demeanor of the wit·
nesscs while testifying, there was reasonable doubt in the minds of
the Commissioners of the guilt of the accused, it was their duty
to give him the benefit of that doubt and to return a verdict of not
guilty. In any event, it was the duty of the Commissioners after
consultation and deliberation to rctu rn a verdict of either "guilty"
or "not guilty" and the Master should have insisted upon a vote being taken by ballot in accordance with the provisions of the constitution.

1st. Charges having been preferred by the Junior \Varden could
the Master of the Lodge take and prosecute an appeal?
2nd. vVas there anv decision bv the Commission
judgment could be based?
.

Oil

which a

3rd. If not, what further proceedings should be had?
Upon the second question the committee was unanimously of
the opinion that there was no verdict or
but was divided
upon the other two questions. The majority was of the opinion that
the appeal was well taken. and hcing thcmseln:s convinced from
their examination of the record that the accused was guilty of the
offense charged, recommended that he b<: suspended by Grand Lodge.
Brother Francis E. Baker, who made a minority report, was of the
opinion that the Junior \Varden was the only party who could appeal,
but that if further proe<'edings \Vere to be had the case should be
remanded to the lodge which tried the case, assigning as a reason
that the accused was entitled to he tried bv a Commission and
that until a verdict by a Commission was rend~red the Grand Lodge
could not have jurisdiction to consider the case upon its merits.
The reports of the Committee on Appeals and Grievances were
not acted upon by Grand Lodge. but were referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence. That committee concurred fully with the majority of the Committee on Appeals and Grie\·ances that the appeal
was well taken; but upon the question of what further proceedings
should be taken agreed with Brother Baker that a trial should be
had and verdict rendered hy a Commission elected from the members of the lodge to which the charges were presented, and that
Grand Lodge had no jurisdiction to consider a case upon its merits
until a trial Commission had rendered a verdict thereon.
The report of the Committee on Jurisprudence was concurred
in by Grand
and that is now the law of this jurisdiction
and has been incorporated into our constitution. Section 208 provides as follows: "Grand Lodge has no power over case until trial
Commission has acted."
ln view of the law of the case by which we are bound, it is
11111wcc·ssary to review the testimony. In this connection, however,

There has, however, been no verdict and the charges are still
pending. The Commission has been discharged; a new Commission
must therefore be elected.
The onlv doul;t is with reference to the fourth question propounded bv -the ::Vfaster: "Can tlie record of the first trial, or the
evidence t;ken by deposition, with or without the consent of the
parties be htid before, or in any way used by, the new Commission?"
At first blush it would seem as though the question. should be
answered in the negative. Among other objections which might he
urged against such a procedure is the fact that the new Commis·
sioners will not be afforded an opportunity of observing the demeanor
of the witnesses while
or the manner in which the testimony is given. In view, however, of the fact that the records and
reporter's transcript of testimony made in courts of the land, properly authenticated, may be received in evidence, there seems to hie
no good reason why testimony taken at a Masonic trial of the accused,
reduced to writing, signed by the witnesses and properly certified
and authenticated. should not he likewise admissible in a rc·trial of
the case upon the original charges, which nmM be deemed to be
still pending.

and uninfluenced by . mercenary motives he freely and voluntarily
offered himself as a candidate for the mysteries of Masonry; that he
was prompted to solicit this privilege by a favorable opinion conceived of the institution, a desire for knowledge, and a sincere wish
to be serviceable to his fellow creatures." That is a wonderful declaration-a fundamental statement of a great faith in an institution. Has,
to you and me, that faith been realized? For a personal answer to
that question I go back forty years and more in my own experience.
As I do so I feel sure that many of you will travel with me ova
forgotten roads of memory and that you will wander in bypaths of
forgotten experiences, and that possibly you, like myself, will find
a sufficient answer to the question.
::\fy first impressions of Free Masonry were indeed boyish but
have been lasting. They were received when, as a mere lad my father
held me by the hand, at the funeral of one dear to my family; a man of
standing and influence in the community. One of the then Grand
Wardens of this Body, a dear and intimate friend of him who had
gone, by special request, had come from his distant home to conduct
the funeral ceremonies according to the ritual of the order. He acted
as the Master of the Lodge upon that occasion and his presence there
created comment, for even then, although young in years, he was
being honored by the people of the State. He was my father's friend
and I looked up to him as being a great man.
The village preacher was there, acting as chaplain of the Lodge:
"A man he was to all the country dear."
Often did I hear him in his strong denunciation of sin and the
sinner; as often did I shudder at his portrayal of an angry God;
but more often did I run at his kindly call to have him lay his hand
upon my head and out of the kindness of his great loving heart talk to
me as one boy to another. He was loved in the community, for he
never turned aside from the call of distress. Where sickness was, he
was there:
"Beside the bed where parting life was laid,
And sorrow, guilt, and pain, by turns dismay'cl,
The loving champion stood."
The village schoolmaster was there. He wore his white apron,
the badge of a l\faster Mason, with the same simplicity with which
he went about his daily task. He, too, was love cl and revered in that
community ancl of him it might be said as Goldsmith sang, of that
other schoolmaster of the deserted village:
"And still they gazed and still the wonder grew
That one small head could carry all he knew."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

187

The Judge from the neighboring county seat was also there, a
man of probity and uprightness; and though stern, recognized as just.
The strong men of the county grouped around that humble abode-the
men who were the backbone am! sinew of the community. The Holy
Bible was borne forth by the eldest member of the Lodge, and as
it passed supported hy the Deacons with their rods, a hush seemed to
fall on the place. 1t was a tribute, to my boyish mind, to the word of
Goel. Those early impressions remained with me as I grew into manhood. I had a simple faith in, coupled perhaps with a youthful curiosity to learn more of, this to me, mysterious order.
I became a man; I kno~ked and the door of Free Masonry was
opened unto me. Within the Lodge I met men who called me
"Brother.'' I felt that my boyish ambitions were about to be realized;
that my dreams were al1out to come true. As a novitiate I received
instruction. I learned that the three principal tenets of Masonry are
Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth. I saw men reverently bow their
heads and invoke the blessing of God that He would so influence their
hearts and minds that they might practise out of the Lodge those
great moral duties inculcated in it. In the outer world I saw Masons
in high places in political and official lifd, administering the affairs
of the State and Nation, with honor and uprightness. I saw justice
tempered with mercy and guided hy "that standard, or boundary of
right which enables ns to render unto every man his just clue, without
distinction." I .saw the man of Goel soften his dogmatic creeds with
the doctrine of universal love. I saw men leading little children tenderly along the pathways that lead to truth, and fighting valiantly for
the rights of childhood. I saw my brethren occupying positions of
honor, integrity and trust, and everywhere regarding the volume of
the Sacred Law as the great light of their profession-considering it
as the unerring standard of truth and justice, and regulating their
actions by the divine precepts it contains.
When I was Master of my Lodge there came to us, to lay the
cornerstone of a public building, a beloved Grand Master of this
jurisdiction. He performed the impressive ceremonies of the occasion with dignity. Later at a gathering in his honor, standing upright
in our midst he made an appeal to his Brethren of the Craft to be
men. It was a strong cry, uttered from the heart of a strong man. It
made a deep and lastin[ impression upon the throng of Masons there
assembled. Standing in the full height of his physical manhood and
with a voice like that of a prophet calling to his children to follow
him, he closed with the beautiful words of Doctor Holland:

J\Ien who possess opinions and a will;
:\Ten who have honor,-mcn who will not lie;

In his annual address at this Commnnication, onr Most Worshipful
Grand Master has allnclccl with deep feeling to the personnel of onr
Craft in this jurisdiction. He has dwelt at length upon the· calibre
of the men who comprise the membership of our order in this state.
I know that he is justified in his high estimate of these men. As we
journeyed together throughout the length of the jurisdiction, as we
met these men, as we lookccl into their faces around the festal board,
or rcposccl in their homes as their honorcfl gn<:sts or met them in

and I assert that the rank and file of the Masons in this state measure
up to the cry of the poet, so beautifully expressed in the words quoted
by the Grand Master, now deceased, "Goel give us men!"

It is not in the material achievements of our Order that the
greatest results of its teachings are to be found. Our success rests
not in stately edifices of brick, and mortar, and wood, and steel, and
stone, hut in influence on the minds and hearts of men. The g4eatest
monuments to the success of the institution arc to he found in the
work carried on by it in furtherance of that "sincere wish to be serviceable to his fellow creatures" expressed in the petition of each Master
Mason. Service of the distressed worthy Brother, the protection and
care of his widow and orphan, the good counsel whispered in his ear,
the admonition of his errors, the efforts for his reformation, and the
inspiration of his soul to better things and to immortality-these are
the greatest of its achievements. This may be expressed far more
beautifully than I, in my own language, might tell it, in a little story
by Professor I-I enry Van Dyke, which I have a number of times during
the year used to illustrate this point. I had not intended to repeat it

GHAND LODGC: OF CALIFOHNIA

189

here, hut, at the request of a number of the brethren, and with
apologies for its repetition, I will again tell it.
It is "The Story of the Other \Vise Man," Artiban, the Median,
who in the clays when Augustus Caesar was master of many kings,
and Herod reigned in Jerusalem, dwelt in the City of Ecbatana. in a
heantifd garden watered by the streams descending from the slopes
of l\lt. Orantes. and made mnsical by innumerable birds. He was one
of the ancient priesthood of the l\I;.gi. called the "Fire Worshipers."
Tt had been revealed to him and to his three companions, Caspar,
Melchior and Balthasar, in the ancient tablets of the Chalclees, thJt
a new star would appear, whicl1 would herald the birth of one who
should he born of the King of Israel, one who should point the way to
all Truth.
...
Artaban sold his house and his possessions and bought three
jewels to carry them as a tribute to the King. Thev were wonderful
gerns-"one blue as a fragment of the night sky, o~e redder than a
ray of sunrise, and one as pure as the peak of a snow mountain at
twilight."
vVhile Artaban watched in his home for the coming of the stars.
his three companions were watching at the ancient temple of the
Seven Spheres in BaLylonia. Artahan called many of his friends together and showed them his precious gems, told them of the coming
of the star, and asked them to accompany him. !mt one and all, thev
turned aside am\ Artaban was left in solitude. As he watched "fa.r
over the eastern plain a white mist stretched like a lake. But where the
distant peak of Zagros serrated the western horizon the sky was clear.
Jupiter and Saturn rolled together like drops of lambent flame about
to blend in one. Artaban bowed his head. He covered his brow with
his hands. 'It is the sign,' he said. 'The King is coming, and I will
go to meet him.' "
All night long he rode westward on Vascla, the swiftest of his

Our brother in '1is relations to humanity keenly felt this sense
of responsibility and it cat'.sed him to consecrate his life to the
highest ideals. Realizing thnt through the ages man has ever been
the dupe of those who would prey upon his superstitious fears through
dogmatic and ·false religions, he foug·ht with all the fire of his entlmsiastic nature to combat a power \vhich he implicitly believed to
be inimical and in violent opposition to those basic principles upon
which rests the perpetuity of American Liberty.
Brother Sherman's humanitarianism caused him to cry out for
freedom of individual action in regard to religion and politics; to
decry against the political power of any Church or creed in the
governmental affairs of this, or any other nntion; and as a great
bulwark against the encroachment of such political hierarchical machina.
tions he fought with all the ardor of his great soul for universal nonsectarian educational institution~.
His Masonic life w:c<s marked by vitalized activity, for he served
in nearly all the offices of Blue Lodge. Chnpter of Royal Arch, Council
of Royal and Sdcct :\!asters, and Scotti:;h Rite, demitting frequently
from one body at his last place of
to hccomc a member
or charter member of another hotly, where he took up his new
abode. In this wav he was
identified with ;\fasonic Bodies
all over the Pacifi: Ccast from San Diego to Seattle; aurl even the
mining towns 'of X evada and California were bencGtc<l by his untiring labors and his cnr eloquent yoke.
His writings and his speeches, sometimes
from his
excess of zeal, were ever and always permeated with the desire to
inspire men to activity in a cause which he thought was necessary
to the salvation of his country. ·Vigorously and unsparingly did he
flay those whom he con:.iderec\ its enemies; yet his heart was always as tende1- as that of a little child. In all the annals of Masonry there are frw i11stances that furnish a nobler example of genuine,
~isinterested and exalted loyalty to principle and to Masonry as the
hfe of Brother Edwin Allen Sherman.

To the M.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee to whom was referred Trial Record No. 163 of
Alturas Lodge No. 248, F. & A. :\I.. suspended by said Lodge on
August 8th, 1914, for unmasonic conduct, begs leave to report as
follows:
The accused was charged in a single specification with the offense
of unmasonie conduct. Because of the very serious character of the
charge made, your Committee has given the record more than usual
consideration, but is forced to the conclusion that, considering the
character of the evidence offered to support the charge, there may
have been a gross miscarriage of justice.
The only evidence that tends even remotely, in the opinion of
your Committee, to sustain the charge is purely hearsay, and for that
r~ason, under the repeated rulings of our Grand Lodge, was inadmissible and is therefore entitled to no consideration. The rernainini:;
evidence not only is insufficient to sustain the charge made, but by
reason of its nature creates a suspicion against the good faith of the
prosecution.

The accused, in his answer to the charge states that he was
unable to attend the trial at Alturas on account of lack of necessary

with his wife and two lioys. He also states that he was unsuccessful
in obtaining the sen·ices of a hrother lo present his defense, although
he applied to three, but the record shows that he was represent_ed o_n
the trial by a brother, although no evidence was introduced 111 !us
behalf.
\Vhile there is some competent evidence which might, if true.
sustain a less serious charge than the one specified, your Committee
is oi the opinion that this evidence is capable of either explanation or
successful refutation and therefore believes that justice requires that
the accused should at least be gh·en a hearing in his defense and for
that reason your Committee offers the following resolution:
Rcsohicd, That the action of ,\ltnras Lodge ;.Jo. 248 in suspendin~

A very pleasing feature of the installation of the Grand
Master was the presentation on behalf of the Southern
California Past :\fasters· "\ssociation of a gavel suitably
inscribed, the head of said gavel being made from a piece
of fossil bone from the Rancho La Brea, where excavations
are being made under the direction of the Board of Governors of the l\I useum of 1-1 istory, Science and Art of Los
Angeles. "The head of the gavel is unique in character
and existed in life long before there was any trace of
human life on this Coast. ] t is from the caudal vertebra
of the giant ground sloth, perhaps one of the most striking
animals in aprearance from the asphalt beds. During the
Pleistocene Period, some two hundred thousand years ago,
this species roamed in great numbers in South America,
reaching the southern part of the United States during the
above mentioned period. He was among the heavyweights,
for he must have tipped the scales at about 4000 pound-;.
The tail of which this vertebra was a part acted as a third
leg when he rose to tower above his kind."

was received with great applause.

noted for its conservatism, its respect and reverence for tradition,
for established usages and laws," and that in this age when there is
such a growing unrest and ofttimes a cr;l\·ing for change and a demand
for so-called "progress," J\lasonry constitutes a bulwark of social
and civic safety; and these are among the reasons why there should
be no yielding to this modern fancy for a General Grand Lodge, and
while these "Annual Conferences," five or six of which have already
been held, have always disclaimed the purpose of promoting the idea
oi a General Grand Lodge, yet in the language of the immortal Bard
of Avon, ":VIethinks she doth protest too mnch," and if there is no
purpose to propagate a General Grand Lodg·e idea, wherein lies the
necessity of 'Yiasons, bearing "Past Grand" titles, getting together each
year in elaborate conventions to thrash over the same old straw that
is thrashed at every one of these meetings? Some of those who have
been wont to assemble in these annual conferences, have
been more frank than others, and have openly espoused the General
Grand Lodge idea. and in one of the Cr~mcl Lodge reports, Oregon we
believe, the Grand Master reported the proceedings of the Indianapolis meeting under the caption in large letters in his report "GENERAL GRAND LODGE."
• It will. of course, be utterly impossible to create a General Grand
Lodge. Masonic tradition and sentiment, and :\fasonic Landmark;
are all against this proposition, nevertheless, in our judgment no good
arises from these annual conferences and Grand Lodges generally
ought to discourage them.

THE LITERARY EXCELLENCIES OF

The literary character of many of the annual addresses of Grand

repay any person's time devoted to their perusal. \Vithout invidious

The Committee on Jnri;;prudence of the Grand Lodge of N'cw
York this year makes this statement concerning this subject:
The subject of a General Grand Lodge in North America, and
particularly one embraced within the territorial limits of the
United States of America, has been frequently agitated. It was
first presented to this Grand Lodge nearly a hundred years ago; the
brethren who were then in life and active in the affairs of the
Fraternity gave it much study and consideration, but, believing it
not to be for our interest, declined to join in the movement. Their
attitude, together with that of the larger Jurisdictions. ended
the matter for a while, but the project has been revived a number
of times since, always with the same result. N cw York has
consistently held to its own sovereignty as an independent Grand
Lodge.
Your committee sees no reason why we should recede from that
position, and therefore recommends that no action be taken in
the matter. We arc now supreme in all things :Masonic within the
borders of the commonwealth of New York. Our authority here
is undisputed, and the brethren direct and control their own
affairs. To all yourselves with a General Grand Lodge, having
jurisdiction over all or a considerable portion of English-speaking
North America would be simply to surrender the power and
authority which is now ours, into the keeping of those who would
nece;;;sarily have but little appreciation of our local conditions

for a moment in saying that the effect of such action is to deny

As \.VC assemble in this, the Xinety-third Annual Comnmnication of this Grand

California, 1912, is fraternally considered and complimentary
allusion made to the extremely generous nature of the relief work
performed in this jurisdiction.
He observes that we work upon what was called (from its place
of origin), the "\Visconsin" plan, which is that the Lodge to which
the brother belongs is bound to relieve his necessities, wherever he may
be. He dissents from this method and holds. that it is the duty of
every Mason to relieve a brother applying to him, if the applicant is
worthy,
far as he can do so without injury to himself.
So do we. So does California, and this is now and always has
been the practice in California, and relief has never been contingent
upon reimbursement by the brother's home Lodge, as may be clearlv
found from the hundreds of thousands of dollars paid out by ou~
Boards of Relief in this State for which no reimbursement has ever
'-iccn made, and in thousands of cases never even thought of; but

California holds, and justly holds, that if a distressed brother's Lodge,
to which he has perhaps paid dues for many years, is able to make~
reimbursement for advances to relieve his distress, such reimbursement
is right and proper.

27

gethcr, to work more in harmony, and to understand each other
better. The conferences of Grand l\lasters in the United States
appear to produce good results.
The steady, i;egular growth of the order in numbers is really
remarkable. There is not a Grand Lodge in the world which does
not report an increase of strength. At the same time there is
evidence on every hand of greater carefulness in the selection of
material. The standard of membership rises year by year.
Masonic benevolence is more carefully watched than formerly.
While the amounts given to the needy steadily increase in volume,
greater care is exercised in systematizing the charities and cuttingoff impostors. It is not possible wholly to prevent fraud, but system and co-operation do much toward that end.
On the whole, Masonry never stood so high as a worker of
good, and never exercised so beneficial an influence on the world's
thought and the world's morality, as it docs now when it approaches the end of the second century of its existence as an
organized body.
It is much to be regretted that several reports have failed
to reach the committee in time for review this year. At the time
when the printer thinks the copy must be "all in" the Proceedings
of the Grand Lodges of Arizona, Costa Rica, Cuba, Montana, New
York, South Australia and Victoria have not been received.
All of which is fraternally submitted.

CONNECTICUT.

1914.

The One Hundred and Twenty-sixth Annual Communication of
the l\Iost Worshipful Grand Lodge of Connecticut, A. F. & A. M. was
held at Masonic Temple, in the city of Hartford, commencing February
4, A. D. 1914, A. L. 5914, at 11 a. m., Grand Master Wilbur S.
Comstock presiding.
Grand Master Comstock sets forth in a concise and business-like
manner his official activities within the year. He· refers to the Conference of Grand Masters held 111 1913, at Indianapolis. He was unable to attend, but ·expresses himself concerning these meetings as
follows:
Such conferences ought to prove of value, and the interchange of ideas among the different rulers of the Craft would
seem to furnish the most practical means of securing uniform
legislation by the different Grand Lodges upon important points.
While some have expressed a fear that such conferences are but
an entering wedge towards the formation of a General Grand
Lodge with sovereign powers, we do not share such fears. It is a
historical fact that this has in the pas·t been attempted in vain.
In any event, all Grand Lodges can (and most of them probably
will) easily and successfully refuse to surrender their sovereignty.
He also refers to the invitation, which he was unable to accept, to
attend the George Washington Masonic Memorial Association, held at
Alexandria, Va., on the 22nd of February, 1913. Concerning this
organization, he expresses himself as follows :
The object of this organization was originally to provide
a fire-proof building in which the priceless relics of Brother
George Washington, now in the possession of Alexandria-Washington Lodge, might be preserved, and secure their removal from the
old and insecure building where they are now kept. Gradually the
scope of the movement grew until it now includes the erection of
a Memorial Temple, the title to wbich is to be vested in the
association, now a permanent organization, and thus to be owned
by the entire fraternity of the United States. With these objects,
I am in lively sympathy and trust that this Grand Lodge will be
fully represented at the February meeting of the association.
From the report of the Grand Secretary, we observe that $1468
was contributed to the Wes tern Flood Fund; certainly an excellent
showing for a jurisdiction no larger than Connecticut.
In accordance with the recommendation of the Committee on
Foreign Correspondence, fraternal recognition was extended to the
Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands.
The following resolution was adopted:
No brother subject to a Jurisdiction which is not recognized by
the Grand Lodge of Connecticut shall be admitted to any Lodge,
unless

REPORT ON tORRESPO);DENCK

First: he is duly vouched for, or unless his certificate shows
that he has been initiated according to the ancient rites and ceremonies in a Lodge professing belief in the Grand Architect of the
Universe, and
Second: not unless he himself shall acknowledge that this belief is an essential landmark of the Fraternity.
Provided: that nothing in the foregoing shall be construed as
allowing the admission of a brother who is subject to any Jurisdiction against which an edict of non-intercourse has been, or
shall be, issued, while such edict is in force. Nor shall it be construed in favor of any member of a clandestine Lodge.
The jurisdiction of Connecticut is in a thrifty and prosperous
condition. The total membership now approaches the 25,000 mark, the
exact number being 24,815, which is ,;n increase over the preceding
year of 611.

The obligations which will he imposed on all Lodges under
this new constitution arc the following:
(1) While the Lodge is at work the Bible will always be
open on the altar.
(2) 'The ceremonies will be conducted in strict conformity
with the Ritual of the "Regime Rectifie" which is followed by
these Lodges, a Ritl'al which was drawn up in 1778 and sanctioned in 1782, and with which the Duke of Kent was initiated
in 1892.
(3) The Lodge will always be opened and closed with the
invocation and in the name of the Great Architect of the Universe. All the summonses of the Order and of the Lodges will
be printed with the symbols of the Great Architect of the Universe.
( 4) No religious or political discussion will be permitted in
the Lodge.
( 5) The Lodge as snch will never take part officially in any
political affair, but every incliviclnal brother will preserve complete liberty of opinion and action.
(6) Only those brethren who arc recognized as true brethren
by the Grand Lodge of England will be received in Lodge.

Georgia has produced a long line of illustrious and eloquent
Grand :\!asters and Grand Master Colding is entitled to stand m the
front rank of these virile and splendid men.
The following is from the opening of his annual address:
In e\'erv man there is some good. In tracing the history of
great crimi1;als it is not unusual to discover that they were once
possessed of capabilities for good, but when the hour of destiny
struck. the fated hour that was to determine whether the soul
should he a maj cs tic riwr tlowing between orderly banks or the
devastating flood, mad, rioting through the land, the hand of gentle
guidance was absent and it became a destroying force of anarchy.
It would have been strange indeed had Ishmael loved his Kind!
Just as the tiny twig at brink of mountain spring may dominate
the course of a giant stream, so may one little act of brotherly
love steer a soul to blessed Heaven.
Man is a social, domestic creature, but a dependent one, and if
denied his natural vent his moral parts are dislocated. Indifference is the monster paralysis. chilling alike the veins and arteries
of social man, a withering blight, choking his aspirations, checking
impulses and enen·ating energv. It is a cold November wind, settling with haggard palor upmi the landscape with that sad effect
we have noted on faces which are not old but aged. It overcasts
the hounding ]Jrow of joy; quenches the e!oquent lightness of the
CY<'; lrns!ws the mnry music of laughter with rude stoppage as we
have seen nature frozen into stolidity by sudden swirl of winter's
wind. lt ndthcr climbs nor falls, but, suspended betwixt animation and death, drips its upas moistme on all around. l\lasonry
detests and shuns this miasmatic debilitation.
The first thing God said, in creation, was "I,et there be light."
He loved brightness then; loves it now, and Masonry is the sun of
exhauMlcss radiance, uplifting man and making him more closely
related to his Creator.

eye clear to see the right, the hrain calm to weigh it and the heart

with no lighter hand applies the punishment.

Jn compliance with the provisions of the Constitution and By-Laws
of the Most vVorshipful Grand Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of Illinois, the seventy-fourth ammal meeting, was
held in the city of Chicago, at M cdinah Temple, conm1cncing on Tuesday, the 14th day of October, A. D. 1913, A. L. 5913, at 10 o'clock a. m.,
and was opened in Ample Form by the M.". \V.". Grand Master, Delmar
D. Darrah.

Grand .:\faster Darrah, in his annual address, felicitates the Craft
upon the high degree of prosperity that exists in Illinois.
The growth in membership has been almost phenomenal, the total
membership now exceeding 122,000, showing a gain of more than 7,000
over the preceding year, with more than 800 active Lodges on the rolL
He reports having issued dispensations for the formation of eleven
new Lodges; Ire dedicakd eleven Masonic halls in person and four
deputy; he laid cornerstones of at least two :Vfasonic temples, several
hospitals, one library, t\vo high school buildings, etc.
Concerning the tendency to invade the prerogatives of subordinate
Lodges by the Grand Lodge the Grand Master has this to say:
One frequently hears complaints that there is too much interference with the affairs of Lodges
the Grand Lodge. The statement is frequently made that to
Lodge should he left the regulation of its household and that to it belongs a certain amount of
individual lil:crty. Ko truer stat<>ment was ever made, but it should
he limited with the proviso that so long as the Lodge is performing the legitimate labors of Masonry it should not be molested.
Freemasonry is a society whose procedures are peculiarly its own.
Today it suffers much from the injection into it of the practices
of other societies. ''fhc Lodge which understands Masonry and
observes its fnndamental principles docs not need to worry on
account of interference. It is the Lodge that is trying to stage
the spectacular and unusual. that is spending its funds extravagantly and for purposes that are not ".\fasonic, that is always seek~
ing an eyasion of the regulations of the fraternity that feels the
chastening rod. Brethren who desire to maintain an existence
under a charter from the Grand Lodge of JIJ.inois must be willing
to be observant of those procedures and practices which distinguish
Masonry and, failing to do so. need not be surprised at interference
with their unmasonic frivolities.

Brother Block in his "foreword," referring to '.\[asonry, remarks
that, while Masonry possesses a measure of perfection in the purpose it
professes, it nevertheless is a human institution ancl must be influenced by the march of progress.
We quote from his introduction as follows:
Masonry is a human institution and despite its great achievements can no more keep from being influenced by the march of
human progress than can any other man-made institution. Even the
great Church of Rome that in one age burned poor Joan of Arc
at the stake as a heretic, was forced in coming years. hy the march
of man's onward and upward movement, to canonize her as a saint.
The progress of J\Iasonry, with all its rigid conscn·atism and
with all its hard-shell adherence to the ancient landmarks has
been slow to be sure, bnt for that very slowness its progress has
been all the more sure. For by her very care and caution, by her
steadfast devotion to a wealth of experience glcanetl from the
records of the past, she has saved poor humanity from falling
into the many pitfalls that beset man's onward road, kept him
from straying into the by-paths of inviting error that lead to sure
and certain disaster. Yea. the world is moving, and :\fasonry ls
moving with it! If she has lee\ more often than she has followed,
this has been due to her constant exaltation of higher ideals of
human life, and her cvcrgrowing loyalty to the high standards
she has raised.
And in his conclusion, or "afterword," he makes some fine observations, from part of which we quote as follows:
We believe that every great institution is entitled to be judged
by the lives, ideals, and aspirations of its leaders and master
si;iirits. For these are the men who put into words and deed the
aims and purposes of the great body of brothers who have elevated
them into positions of guidance and command. These arc they who
have been selected by the brethren to direct the great work of
establishing upon the earth those cherished principles dear to the
heart of every craftsman-selected because of their will and ability
!o work into the life of humanity the great aims, hopes, and
ideals of the Fraternity.

It may be supposed by some of the era ft that these conferences of Grand l\Iasters are "something new 1·nckr the sun" and

His reference to the Masonic Home, which is the one thing in
which ::\fis:rnuri Masons particularly take pride, shows that he is in
cordial sympathy with the institution. This is what he says:
(

'·Year after year the Freemasons of ::\1issouri have pointed with
added pride to this splendid and practical eYidence of Masonic
charitv. I have alwavs felt a deep interest in the Home, have
visiterl it often, and for the past four years have attended nearly
cnry meeting of the board in my capacity as ex-officio member.
These \'isits were not only a duty hut a pleasure as well. The Masonic II ome is the highest expression of the true Masonic spirit in
our Jurisdiction. All have contributed; but what are silver and
gold when weighed in the bahmce against human life and
well-being? lf our contributions to this great work had availed to
bring peace and comfort to only one aged man or women and to
smooth the pathway to the grave. is there one of us who would
withdraw his gift, were it possible. and leave the helpless to die
in wretcheduess and want? Or. if only one child, orphaned and
helpless, had been protected and cherished, educated and trained
to a useful life. is there one amongst us who would regret the cost
to him?"

In his reference to the "Melting Pot" may be found a trace of the
proud and ancient faith to which he belongs :
Our Fraternity may well be compared to a melting pot or
crucible in which the various elements of our population may be
fused into one common mass, and the figure is not inapt. vVhen we
consider the manv classes and conditions of men that are daily
landing on our shores and becoming part of our national life,
we can easily see that any influence which tends to remove from
them the dross of ignorance and prejudice, belonging to their old
conditions. and bringing them into sympathy with our own institutions, is most useful and worthy. \Vhatever of antagonism exists
between races and classes is most unfortunate, and of all societies,
Freemasonry is especially called and fitted for assimilation work.
Its genial spirit should thaw into streams of sympathy the icy
barriers which too often separate men, and unite them into one
common band of friends and Brothers; and, failing in this, it
signally fails in one of its missions. If this be true, how strange
to hear or to know of Lodges into which men of certain faiths
are denied admission ; or even more strange, a Lodge at whose
door a policeman, a fireman or a letter carrier knocks in vain!
A Lodge erecti1~g such barrier or holding such prejudices is manifestly lacking in that broadness of thought and feeling which should
characterize everv member of our Fraternity. Let us hope that
wherever such sp'irit may now exist it will soon disappear forever.
Intelligence and good moral character may be found in all the
walks of life. Freemasonry should regard no man for his worldly
wealth or honors. \tVith education, as now generally diffused,
there is no occasion for caste.

The Twenty-fourth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
K cw Zealand was held at Auckland, J\Iay 14 and 15, 1913, M." · W." ·
Brother Maurice Thompson, Grand l\Iaster, presiding.
The session opened with a large attendance and the usual annual
business was transacted.
The jurisdiction of New Zealand is prosperous and thrifty. It has
193 active Lodges with an aggregate membership of nearly 13,000.
A proposition was advanced that the Grand :\faster be elected
biennially, hut failed of adoption. It was decided that the future communications of the Grand Lodge be held in \V cllington, instead of
meeting in different places as heretofore.
The most far-reaching matter considered and adopted was a memorandum of agreement between the Grand Lodge of Kew Zealand and

l

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

109

the Grand Lodge of Scotland, by which the latter Grand Lodge recognizes the full sovereignty and independence of K cw Zealand. Scotland
is loathe to yield territory or concede the right of her subordinate
Lodges to organize into independent Grand Lodges, and it has always
been the practice of Scotland to refuse recognition to these newly
formed Grand Lodges until her opposition became in a sense absurd and
ridiculous, and it is only after these newly formed Grand Lodges acquire sovereignty by prescription, as it were, that Scotland finally yields
consent.
This is practically the case of New Zealand, and there is very little
virtue in Scotland agreeing to recognize N cw Zealand after that j urisdiction had acquired a sufficient standing to laugh Scotland in the face.
The Report on Correspondence is by l\I.". \V.". Brother Alfred H.
Burton, Past Grand :\faster.
Bro'ther Burton in his introduction refers to the large American
Lodges, particularly Palestine Lodge in Detroit, Michigan, and certain
other Michigan Lodges. and wonders if these Lodges arc organized for
the purpose of exemplifying Symbolic l\Iasonry or are simply used as
an "avenue to lead the unwary to a something which is not Ancient
Freemasonry at all, but is just perhaps a theological excrescence."
Brother Burton possibly fails to comprehend the fact that in
America things are done in a large way and that it is characteristically
American to bore with a big augur, and that these large Lodges arc
just as truly l\Iasonic as the smaller ones, and arc not used simply as
a gateway into the so-called higher degrees.
Brother Burton in his report reviews California, 1912, with intelligent judgment and has favorable comment for practically all that California did l\Iasonically in the preceding year.
M.". w:. BRO. l\L\uRICE THOMPSON, of Tnvercargill, Grand l\fastcr.

The Cram! ,\I askr ma(k ;1 stirring address. in which he paintctl in
glowing color,.; the progrc;;s of the Fraternity in South Australia.
He rcfL•rred to the many tokens of n·,.;ped which he ha<! received,
and recounted a numhcr of the inspiring incidents which had occurred
in his experience in South Australia, and breathed the hope that the
fotme would be as grand and glorious as the past.
The Pro. Cram! Master, :'.\ [. ·. \V. ·. Brother Eustace Beardoe
Cnmdy, K. C., made a brief address, in which he expressed the utmost
lrlyalty to the Grand Master and to the fraternity of South Australia.
The Board of General Purposes. which is the real executive board
of the Grand Lodges of Australia, made its report, showing the progress of the Craft and its general condition of prosperity.
The Board reports that the past year had been an exceedingly busy
one. warrants for nine new Lodges were granted; five had already
been consecrated, <tml it was the expectation that the remaining four
would be consecrated in a very short time.
There arc now 77 Lodges in acth·c work, with a total membership
of o\·er 5,000.
The reports of the yarions Funds are very satisfactory and dis·
closed a sound financial condition of the jurisdiction .
There is a Report on Foreign Corre;;pondcnce, prepared by a committee of fourteen, the report of each jurisdiction being initialed by
the member of the committee making the review of that jurisdiction.
California, 1913, ls reviewed by Brother :F. Lathlean. Grand Master Filmer is commended for the high Masonic note struck in his address. Brother Fi!rnC"r's activity in visiting subordinate Lodges is particularly praised and especial reference is made to the fact that he
visited not kss than 61 Masonic districts representing over 300 Lodges.
The scholarly address of Grand Orator Hervey is referred to in
terms of strong commendation and several paragraphs are quoted from
the oration.
The Correspondence Report throughout shows much discrimination and original comment.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

It would strike a casual observer that pretty nearly all of the spare
time of the Grand l\faster must be devoted to \veighing the pros and
cons of cases of physical defects.

Some of the decisions accepted without question by our Texas
brethren, produce a feeling of wonderment, even though we believe
that the moral preception of the good people on the Pacific Coast is as
high as exists in the Lone-Star State. For instance, here is one:
It was decided that a Lodge cannot place a billiard or pool table
in a building used for Lodge purposes, nor could they permit dominos
to be played in the anterooms. The Grand Master states that such
would be a gross violation of the l\Iasonic Law, and the Lodge so
off ending could not reasonably hope to retain its charter, "for so long
a single day." As stated above, we wonder why?
Yet, notvvitbstancling this ruling about pool tables and dominos, the
Grand ::\faster held it no impropriety that the ladies of the Eastern
Star, in giving a program of entertainment in the Lodge room, and
rooms adjacent thereto, might indulge in a representation of a Virginia
Reel to be participated in by a few selected couples of the most elderly
members, etc., in other words, "dancing but not dominos."
The Grand Jurisdiction of Texas is a fine jurisdiction, one of the
nry best in the world. It's ;\fasonic Orph~n's Home may be almost
considered, a model of its kind, and the Masonry of Texas is of a
splendid type in every way; so if we observe some trifling peculiarities,
touching the matter of visible physical defects, and express a little
wonderment at some of the so-called decisions, we do not intend therebv
to say a word in
of the magnificent hodv of men who bea.r
aloft the banners
11Iasonry in Texas.
.
After the death of Past Grand Master Thomas M. Matthews, who
for twenty-five years. prepared the annual report on
Correspondence, the position of Correspondent was assigned to Past Grand
Master George W. Tyler.
Brother Tyler is not a novice in this line of work, as he made the
report on Correspondence in 1887. He was at that time chosen Junior
Crancl \Varden and in due time became Grand Master.
His present report is an excellent production in which California,
1912. is considered in a fraternal spirit.

VERMONT.

1914.
The frontispiece of the Proceedings 1s an excellent portrait of
Crand ~laster Eugene S. VI/ es ton.
A Special Communication of the Grand Lodge of Vermont was
held at St. Johnsbury, July 29, 1913, for the purpose of dedicating the
new Masonic Temple erected there by the fraternity.
The dedicatory address was delivered by Hon. C. H. Darling of
Burlington. He gave utterance to some excellent thoughts and we
excerpt from his address as follows:
This is an extraordinary era. The age is restless. It is a
time of discontent, of complaint, and of dissatisfaction. It is a
time when olcl things ancl old ways seem out of place. The Sermon
on the Mount, the Golden Rule, and the Ten Commandments, are
out of fashion. It is an age of fault finding, when every man, like
the Pharisee, thanks Goel that he is not as other man are. Men
feel that their lot in life is hard. and think that forces outside
themselves are the cause. We seek to improve our own conditions
by correcting others. We rarely hear the old Scriptural injunction,
that whom the Lord loveth He chasteneth, or, that contentment
is the key to happiness. The family Bible is no long-er blotted,
blistered. with the tears of those that have found comfort and
rest unto their souls.
NO'L' ,\LL PROGRESS.

Growth implies a change in all the parts. But, unfortunately,
change has become so associated in our minds with growth that
we have confused the real distinction between that which causes
growth and the change which is associated with decay and dissolution, and we are being led to believe that all change is growth,
and we describe it under the general name of progress.
Now, progress is an act of eliminating the useless. So that
the conservative, or one who is guided by the true principles of the
past, is under suspicion, and one who abides in doctrines as sound
as Holy Writ is in clanger of being looked upon as out of elate
and behind the times.

As a matter of information for our American brethren who are
not distressed over the form of a toast to any heredity over-lord or
ruler, the following concerning what is generally known as the "Loyal
Toast," may be of interest:
Since the death of His late Majesty, King Edward VII.
''Protector of the Craft," the question has been widely discussed
as to the proper form of submitting what is generally known as
the "Loyal Toast," and as much difference of opinion has arisen,
] propose to say a few words on the subject for the guidance
of the brethren in the jurisdiction. So important was the question
considered in England that the matter was thoroughly examined
by W.". Bro. J. P. Simpson, Past Assistant Grand Registrar,
who elicited much information of great interest to the Craft. In
the year 1738 the ReY. James Anderson, D. D., compiled the
English Book of Constitutions. He informs us that in 1430 in the
time of King James I, of Scotlaud, this Toast was drunk by the
Lodges in Scotland. St. Joh n's Lodge No. 3, Glasgow, have still
in their possession a celebrated chest which apparently was used
at all great Masonic functions in the 17th century, and to contain
records. Outside is carved "God Save the King and Mason, 1648,"
The next reference is to the laying of the Foundation Stone of
the new banqueting hall at Whitehall in 1607, when a purse of
broad pieces was laid upon the stone for the l\f asons to drink to

,.

153

"The King and the Craft." In 1719 at the Festival of the year,
Dr. Desaguliers, the then Grand Master, renewed the old and
peculiar toasts and healths of Freemasonry, the first again being
"The King and Craft." At the laying of the Foundation Stone of
the Church of St. Martin's, in Campis, in the reign of George I.
1727, the toast of "The King and the Craft" was drunk with full
Masonic honours .. ] n all toast lists, whether in the 18th or 19th
ccnturv this toast holds the foremost place. At the Act of
Union. ~f "The Athol or Anticnts'' and "Senior or Modern" in
1813, the toast was given with foll Masonic honours. The Grand
Secretary of the "Antients" sets out in the minutes of his Grand
Lodge on two occasions the correct toasts to be given. In the
minutes of June, 1760, and again the minutes of September, 1761.
the authorised toast "The King ancl the Craft" he<1cls the list. On
the first date George II was King. ancl on the second George IlI,
and neither of these monarchs were Freemasons. In regard to
the Grand Lodge of Irclancl WC nncl in the Constitution published
in Duhlin in the year 1751, that when the Foundation Stone of
the Parliament House was laid, a great number of Freemasons
were present and the health of "The King and the Craft" was
drunk, and in the Book of Constitutions of the same Grand Lodge
published in 1817, the first toast is that. of "The King and the
Craft." During the lifetime of Her late Majesty Queen Victoria
the first recognised toast was "The Queen ancl the Craft." At
the Festival of the Grand Lodge of England held in May last
year, the Pro Gran cl Master, Lord Ampthill. said, in proposing
the toast:
"Brcthrnn.
gi,·e you the time-honoured toast of "The King
and the Craft," am! perhaps you will allow me just for once in a
while to say that not only is the toast time-honoured. but it has a
meaning which is not understood by all brethren. There are son~e
who think that if thev drink to the King and the Craft they arc m
one and the same h~·eath honouring His Majesty the King and
drinking· prosperity to the Craft. 1 venture to think that is not so.
I think the true significance is this-that, as Freemasons, one of
the first principles we are obliged to practice as citizens of the
world is that of loyalty to the Government under which we live,
and, above all, loyaity to the Sovereign. We cannot in conformity
with our pledges associate ourselves with any men, whether they
be Freemasons or otherwise. or whether they be men of our own
country or in foreign countries, who arc concerned in plots or
c.onspiracics, or who arc undcrmininQ; the monarchy under which
they Ji,·e. That is th',' signincance of the toast. It is a pledge to
which we might Le called upon to prove our sincere attachment, ancl
it is of that I \Vish to rcmincl you."
I agree with everything that Lord Ampthill has said, aml
hope that the first toast of the evenin~ will retain its timchonoured form-"The King and the Craft."

His references to th~ conservatism of Freemasonry, to its influence
in amalgamating the rich and the poor into a homogeneous citizenship;
his appreciation of the fact that the restless spirit of change so rampant
in our social and political life has not been permitted to lay its hands
on our ).fasonic institution, and his understanding of the real reason
for the marvelous success of Freemasonry, are all so cogently set
forth in certain paragraphs of his address, that we take the liberty of
quoting them in full as follows :
Another peculiarity of Masonry is its conservatism, its respect
and reverence for tradition, for established usages and laws. In
this age when there is a growing unrest, a widening disregard
of the principles underlying our democratic institutions, and even
a lessening respect for established law, the conserving influence
of such an institution as ours on our community, state and national
life cannot be estimated.
I believe the greatest problem this country has to solve today
is how to amalgamate the rich and the poor into a common, homogeneous citizenship, by eliminating the arrogance of the one and
the envy of the other. l\Iasonry, perhaps more than any other
single factor, is helping to accomplish this beneficent purpose.
Its teaching that rich and poor belong to a common brotherhood,
who must meet upon a common level, is doing much to beat down
the barriers of caste, and make men in spirit, what they are in
fact, brothers all, descended from a common ancestry, working
for the common weal. and traveling to a common bourn.
The ruthless spirit of chance, so rampant in our social and
political life, must not be permitted to lay its hands on our Masonic institutions. Masonry can only be maintained in its purity
and its essence by unswerving loyalty to the faith of our fathers
and by absolute adherence to our ancient laws and landmarks.
Let us he devoutly thankful for the heritage that has come down
to us through the centuries; let us glory in our antiquity; let us
be proud of the fact that we can trace our lineage back through
the ages to that wonderful race which appears to have been God's
chosen people to bring both Christianity and Masonry to light.
The real reason for the marvelous successs and vitality of
Freemasonry is the fact that it has pursued the even tenor of its
way,. refusing to turn to the right or left, out of the beaten path
our fathers trod. And today in the presence of this distinguished
gathering, representing the flower of Wisconsin Masonry, I know
I voice the universal sentiment when T declare that there must be
110 innovations in the bo<ly of Masonry.

constituent Lodges with his presence within the year.
The following excerpt from the conclusion of his annual address
shows that Masonry is growing and prospering in vVyoming:
Masonry is growing ;ind prospering in \Vyoming, the number
?f the Lodges as well as the membership thereof continues to
tncrease; naturally this increases the labor and responsibility of the
Grand Master, and the past year has been one of great activity

for me, nevertheless, the opportunity for extending my knowledge
of the state and the many delightful people that I have met, have
fully compensated for the labor and time expended,. and' I .shall al'ways look back upon this year as a pleasant spot. 111 my ltfe, only
regretting my inability to do more and better service for .our noble
Order. The experience of the past year has resulted 111 greater
knowledge and more appreciation of Masonry, and I shall step out
of office into the ranks ready to help carry forward the good work
that ~1asonry is endeavoring to accomplish.
On recommendation of the Committee on Correspondence, fraternal recognition was extended to the Grand Lodge of the Philippine
Islands.
A resolution was adopted, the purport of which was the gathering
of information as to the methods pursued in other jurisdictions for
caring for destitute brothers from other jurisdictions.
The report of the Grand Secretary shows a gain in membership of
l 91 over the preceding year, the total memhership at this time being

3,036.
The Report on Correspondence is hy the veteran Grand Secretary,
\V. L. Kuykendall. California, 1912. is fraternally considered, \vith quotations from the report of the Grand l\Iaster and Committee on Correspornlcnce. Brother Kuykernlall's conclusion, which contains information of a general character, is as follows:
\i'/e have a!:tain nearly reached the end of our journey in reviewinl!," the proceeding of all Grand Lod[res which the Grand Lodge. of
\Vvoming has recognized as regular that have come to hand durt1H.~·
thl: past _year, and, as our conclusion t?. rcport.s of 1911 ~nd 1912
related solclv to the question of recogmt1on, neither of wl11ch have

.
A number of Grand Lod8,"cs still 111s1st that a vVorsh1pful Master
cannot fill th;1t position unless he receives the wonderful secrets of
t11c so-called Past Master's Degree, which is conferred before installation instead of after lie has served honestly through his tcrn1
and rcalh· become a Past "'.\Taster. Delaware has declared it to he a
degree s(llcly under its laws when it is well kno\vn that it belongs;
in the Chapter.
Two or three Grand Lodges insist that the \,Yardens must also
receive it before installation, when a child can see that neither of
the111 mav cn·r heconw Master, thus making it more of a farce than
it really ·i~. l\lany Grand Lodges, however, have wisely prohibited
it. and nothing has happened to any l\Iaster or Lodge through svch
prohibition of a useless barnacle.
Its equally useless twin barnacle, the so-called Grand RepreSl'ntative ~"·stern, having no place whatever in Craft Masonry
under its l;lan of organir.ation, which is admitted by everybody,

165

has very wisely been discontinued hy several Grand Lodges, and
should be abandoned by all. as it is well known by all Masons
to be another farce, the perpetuation of which is not worth the
time, labor, paper, and printers' ink used in keeping it up. One
Grand Master recently referred to said excresence on the body of
Craft Masonry by saying that only seven Grand Lodges had representatives. near his Grand Lodge, and that all other places had been
vacant for years, and yet we find that all the Grand Lodges survived, continued 'to thrive, and that peace and harmony prevailed
between them just the same. W c were surprised that said Grand
l\f aster did not recommend, and that some Brother did not move,
to abolish such a useless system.
As we understand it, England and possibly Scotland, Ireland
and some of the Canadian Grand Lodges, permit dual membership,
which allows a man to join and be a member of as many Lodges in
as many jurisdictions as he may desire. We thought Virginia was
the only jurisdiction that permits such, but find that Massachtisetts
has recently adopted it, thereby creating some friction with Vermont, owing to members in latter becoming members of Lodges
in Massachusetts. \Ve already have too many members who fail to
attend meetings of their Lodges except on special occasions. They
should mend their ways in that regard before trying membership in
more than one Lodge at one and the same time. All Grand Lodges
which permit such doubling up of membership are sailing under the
flag of numerical misrepresentation, and makes all statements of
the total number of Masons absolutely unreliable. Recently, Oregon
\visely and correctly turned down the application of an English
Mason living in that state who wanted to join an Oregon Lodge
while retaining his membership in England. And here is another
opportunity for our good Brothers Wroth and Howard to have
New Mexico and Mississippi adopt dual membership because
England has set the pace.
We had selected the transfer of membership law, perpetual
jurisdiction, correspondence between Lodges, and a few other
questions to incorporate in this conclusion, but have concluded to
defer their presentation for the present.
With unbounded loyalty to regular Craft Masonry, and the
powers that be at present managing its affairs wherever existent,
and kind fraternal regards to our Brother reporters, the membership everywhere, and especially to our brethren of Wyoming, we
bring to a close the result of another year's work as a reviewer.
Respectfully submitted,
C. BARNETT, Grand Master, Cody.
W. L. KUYKENDALL, Grand Secretary, Saratoga.

In this com1cction \Ve should ever keep in mind that the true
mission of l\fasonry must be regarded as an essentially practical one,
if tile institution is to survive the clamors and disturbances of this
age. There are too many practical problems in life nowadays, for a
purely spcculatin: or ethical instrumentality to be of substantial force
or avail. In the heavy press of burdens and responsibilities, public
as well as private, social as well as civic, religious as well as economic,
we must be prepared, not to talk round a problem, but to go through it.
Masonry, then, just as men, must descend from the clouds of
abstract reasoning and concern itself with the vital forces of good
and evil right down here among the lives of our people,-their everyday lives-the commonplaces of their existence-the problems that go
not out of recolkction with the setting of the sun-the things determinative of their destinies.
He, therefore, who would make of
l\Tasllnry an efficient machine for the substantial betterment of mankind. must attune his heart as vvell as his ear to the actual needs
of those who are in distress; must he able to grasp the logic of necessity as well of virtue, and must needs know that the problems of my
brother, ·who is in my keeping, did not spring from an ethical condition
and can not be satisfied hy a mere ethical solution.
In this spirit, if we succeed in any appreciable degree in rendering
the tc11nre of the race here on earth happier, more contented and less
di.-;appointing, we will have justified our existence and offered some
reasonable excuse to our minds and consciences for the time and
effort expended in the name of Freemasonry. Jn this spirit, also,
whatever is an enemy to the genuine progress of the race, is an enemy
of ours, whether it be a war, a famine, a misuse of the powers of
wealth or of industry, or even an institution.
The man, then, who can actually acid something to the uplift of
political life, something to the brotherhood of social life. something
to the ethics of commercial life, something to the justice of industrial
lik something to the freedom of religious life, something to the practical cfticicncy of spiritual life,-that man is a Mason, whether he has
cn-r taken onr obligations or not. He who, on the contrary, has not
done some of these things, even in a small and modest way, is not a
:\I a:-;on. no matter how many letters or figures may be seen after his
name, nor how large and inspiring a watch charm may adorn his
,,·aistcoat.
H.emcmber, no trner or more inspiring sentiment was ever voiced
tlrnn that of him who said:

I

I

l

''\Vith deed arnl word and pen,
Thon hast served thy fellow men;
Tbcrdorc, art thou exalted."

In the midst of our communing together over the affairs of the
Craft, \Ve should not he unappreciative of what is aud has been going
on about us in this busy Exposition City. Here, appropriate monuments commemorative of "the greatest liberty ever taken by man with
nature"-the building of the Panama Canal-have been reared, and
all the world has been hidden to come, that the nations of the earth
. might not only pay deserved tribute to this last and greatest of the
wonders of the world, bnt also that opportunity might be had to
receive ocular proof of the successful rebuilding of a great city.
\Ve of the entire State, again, and in no uncertain tones, congratulate our brethren of San Francisco ;-congratulate you upon your
indomitable spirit, your municipal pride, your marvelous achievements.
The history of San Francisco since April 18, 1906, as written upon the
map of California, betokens an ability successfully to cope with the
powers of nature almost unparalleled in the history of the world.
Vivid as arc our recollections of the awful scenes of horror which
followed in the wake of seismic shock and devouring holocaust, we
almost forget your sufferings in our unstintecl and unhesitating admiration of your pluck and fortitude. The streets that seemingly but a
few months ago were strewn with rocks and wreckage. today groan
with the burden of untold thousands passing over them; the mantle
of dust that hung so long about your horizon like a glowering pall,
has given way to rainbows of festival flags that proclaim from almost
every window and house top, the recurrence of the old-time reign of
melody and merriment. The awful stillness that always follows in
the wake of havoc wrought by nature's forces, has been succeeded by
the busy hum of the wheels of industry, bringing wealth and peace
and prosperity.
The towering monuments of steel and concrete, teeming with the
commerce of the Orient and the Occident, now grace our vision where
before our eyes sought in vain for other than twisted iron and tottering walls; the gloom of despair has passed from faces, and the
glorious sunshine of hope beams forth like a beacon light; privation
and want,-ruthless destroyers of lives and ambitions-have been
swept aside by advantage and opportunity; and the great mart of trade,
so lately smitten by the prepotent powers of nature that it seems
if it were but yesterday, in a spirit of almost unconquerable defiance,
has resumed her sway as Queen of the sunlit sea.
We of the South take a pride fn your achievements; they redound
to the credit not only of your city, but of our whole State; they are
a ~art and parcel of the priceless inheritance of California's history,
which we, our children, and our children's chikhen will recount and
rehearse in the years to come.

DISPE~S:\TlONS.

Many requests for dispensations have been received, a detailed
statement of which,• without doubt, will appear in the report of our
Grand Secretary.
Jn this behalf I can not refrain from reporting that I ha \·e denied
a number of requests made of me for the issuance of dispensations
to reballot within a year on rejected ca11clidates. This I have done
because of my· feeling that the right to cast a black hall in a Masonic
Lodge is a sacred right, to which every conscientious 1fason should
be permitted to lay claim, and the responsibility for the use or abuse
of which is a matter entirely between the individual and his conscience.
I have said more than once in response to applications for dispensations that I had no
and would not use my office, to further
any plan whereby it was sought in any way to override a hlack ball
cast by a brother. \Ve are concerned not merely with getting new
material into the Fraternity; we are deeply and vitally concerned with
maintaining the utmost harmony between those who arc already in it.
On every occasion, however, when through correspondence more or
less extensive, or otherwise, I was enabled reasonably to draw the
conclusion that the individual who had cast a black ball did it through
either mistake or inadvertence, which he desired to rectify, or because
of some reason which was no longer operative with him, and that. in
consequence, upon a reballot the box would probahly be clear, I have,
without hesitation, indicated my willingness to cause the issuance of
the desire<l dispensatinn.

DECISIONS.

In accordance with the usual experience of Grand :Masters, I apprehend, during the course of the year I have been in receipt of almost
numberless requests, of more or less importance, for official rulings
upon controverted questions of Masonic propriety and jurisprudence.
Apparently these requests were almost invariably born of a sincere
desire to obtain "further light in :l\Iasonry," and in that spirit I have
endeavored in every instance to give both rule and reason in answer
to inquiry made. Obviously only a few of such replies, those presenting either novelty or great importance, merit report to or consideration
by this Grand Lodge. Such as are presented herewith, and following
the very commendable example set by Past Grand Master Lawler,
have been already by me submitted to the Chairman of our Jurisprudence Committee.
In only one instance was I in receipt of a request for a ruling
on what might be termed a small and querulous controversy. I submit my reply in spite of the trifling importance of the question presented
merely as a suggestion to the brethren of the wisdom of disregarding
the non-essentials in Masonry. A man who is inspired to seek for a
star ought not to permit himself knowingly to stumble over a straw.
I. One of my Inspectors, indicating that the occurrence had
"caused a little feeling" in the community, asked for a "ruling" on a
protest made by "an old Past Master," arising out of the following
sittiation:
""-\ member of the Blue Lodge who was also a member
of the Comman<lery, died and was buried with Masonic honors. The members of his Commandery acted as escort. In
opening the Lodge and conducting the services, a Past Master
uf the Blue Lodge, who was also a member of the Commandery, officiatr(l in the East in the uniform of a Knight Templar,
to which the old Past Master lirM mentioned took exception
011 the ground that no officer of a Blue Lodge shotilcl appear
in the uniform of another branch of the order."

"Strictly speaking, it is probably true that a Past Master
of a Blue Lodge would find no authority for acting as Master
in opening a Blue Lodge, even for the commendable purpose
of escorting the remains of a deceased brother to the grave,
while clothed in the uniform of a Knight Templar. To that
extent I apprehend that the criticism of the old Past Master
referred to in' your letter was well taken.
"In this behalf, however, I can not refrain from venturing the suggestion that there is nothing in such an oc_c~s.ion
or such an occurrence which ought to call for any cnt1c1sm
or fault-finding on the part of anybody. It occurs to me that
no Blue Lodge Mason, with a true regard for the vital and
substantial things which concern our order, would take ei~her
the time o·r the trouble to complain because some Kmght
Templar, who happened to be a Past Master of the Blue Lodge
and who was intending to act as one of an escort to another
Knight Templar, proceeded to open the Blue Lod.ge. in the
absence of the Master~ without divesting himself of !us Templar
regalia. Surely there is nothing in the nature of Knight Templary which would render its habiliments objectionable to any
person, even though he were a Blue Lodge. 1faso1:, a~1d surely
there could be nothing save a very techmcal objection made
against one sitting in the East, under the c_ir~umstances I have
detailed above. If 'the Blue Lodge was w11!111g that the Commandery should act as escort, no member of the Blue Lodge
should have felt constrain"ecl to offer objection to the fact that
a member of the Commandery, in uniform, being called upon,
officiated in the East. There are so many other things of
moment of which our fraternity has to concern itself that I
am truly surprised that one who has heen honored by a seat
in the Oriental Chair should have taken the trouble to make
objection to such a slight and technical invasion, if it be an
invasion, of our ancient customs and landmarks.

"There does not seem to he any probability of a repetition
of this very serious ( ?) Masonic offense, and so I see no
occasion for any ruling other than what has been indicated
hereinabove in the premises."

I answered that if the candidate announced his intention of going
into the saloon business in a short time the Lodge should not confer
the degrees upon him. Having proclaimed his intention of doing that
which would debar him from membership if uninitiated, and would
result in his expulsion if a member, the Constitution of the Grand
Lodge itself should he construed to operate as a rejection, and the
.:\Jaster should at the next regular meeting announce that objection
to the initiation of the candidate had been made. If this objection was
not withdra\\·n within the sixty clays, i. e., if the candidate did not
renounce his intention of engaging in the prohibited business, the objection should become absolute.

III. A candidate who had been rejected, within the twelve months
thereafter presented his petition and was elected. Then the discovery
was made that his petition had been presented prematurely, and the
l\Iastcr's inquiry was: "What shall we do?" I replied:
"In this case, although the petition was presented prematurely, the committee apparently failed to discover that fact
and rendered a favorable report, upon which the petitioner was
elected. The degrees have not yet been conferred upon him,
and obviously he is disqualified to receive them. He should
not he subjected to the burden and odium of a rejection of the
ordinary kind, and it is my judgment therefore that the Master
should direct the investigating committee to make a special
report upon the question of whether or not his petition has been
received prematurely, and if the report he in the affirmative,
that the Master should then direct that the petition may be
withdrawn, pursuant to the provisions of section 104, the fact
of such withdrawal and the reasons therefor to be entered
upon the minutes of the l,odge."

The givi11g of sheepskin certificates, not as a mere gratuity, but as
a reward of merit, so to speak, to all members who pass a satisfactory
exa111ination in open Lodge in the work of the Third Degree, stands
upon a slightly different basis. I do believe however that there is
nothing intrinsically wrong in such a proceed,ing, that it is in nowise
a misuse of the funds of a subordinate Lodge, and can very properly
be classed as in "promotion of fraternal intercourse," expenditures in
aid of which may be made out of the ten per cent social fund under
the terms of Section 89. "Promotion of fraternal intercourse" is a
very comprehensive expression, and as long as a subordinate Lodge, in
good faith, uses the social fund to such an end as that general interest
and increased activity in the work of the order is promoted, it is my
belief that the supervisory powers of the Grand Lodge should be held
in restraint. It is impossible for me to say that the purchase and
bestowing of the certificates above referred to will not contribute to
added zeal, zest and enthusiasm on the part of the Lodge's membership.
Under such circumstances I must accept the judgment of the Lodge in
the premises, and therefore cannot enjoin the procedure complained of.

To adhere to the ruling heretofore announced it becomes necessary
to read the Constitution as if it said a "vote of the majority of the
members present" shall be necessary to elect. By the use of the true
language, however, "a majority of the 1•otcs" (i. e., preferences expressed-ballots cast) it seems clear to me that a very different signitication was intended.

In this conn~ction it is to be remembered that no power lies in
the l\f aster to compel qualified members present to vote by ballot for
officers, and if the construction announced is to be adhered to it could
easily happen that no choice could ever be made, because, a sufficient
number refusing to vote, or voting a blank ballot, no one could secL1 re
a majority of all members present and qualified to vote.
This matter will present itself for consideration very frequently at
the annual elections, and because of this fact should again receive the
attention of the Grand Lodge. It is only lwcause of its importance
that I am constrained to present it here for renewed consideration.

NECROLOGY

XXIII. Insistent effort was made to get me to annul a ruling of
my distinguished predecessor, Past Grand l\Jaster Murphey, which was
approved by the Grand Lodge, but because of motives of obvious propriety, I refused. Nevertheless, I can come to no other conclusion
than that the ruling in question was an erroneous one, and that this
Grand Lodge should recede from it.
Section 135 of the Constitution, having to do with elections in
subordinate Lodges, provides that "a majority of the votes of the members present shall be necessary to elect," and Section 140 provides that
"none but members in good standing whose dues are paid shall be
entitled to vote." Construing the two sections together, Past Grand
Master Murphey ruled that "it requires a majority vote of the members
present, who are entitled to vote, to determine an election."
It will be observed at once that the Constitution does not say, as
indicated by Past Grand Master Murphey, that a majority "vote" of
the members present is necessary to a choice; the language is "a majority of the votes of the members present." The difference, to my mind,
is most significant. When the Constitution refers to the requisite
"majority," of what is it speaking? Not members, as construed by
Past Grand Master Murphey, but of "votes." The word "votes'' means
formal individual expressions of preference by means of ballots or
otherwise. There is no "vote" as the word is here used unless there
is such expression of preference. and a "majority of the votes" means,
to my mind, just what it says, a majority of the expressions of preference, and not a majority of the members present and entitled to vote
but not voting, as heretofore held.

Tt affords me the greatest comfort and gratification to be able to
report to. you that no official of this Grand Lodge has departed his life
since our last Annual Communication. In that respect, at least, our
ranks arc still intact. Other jurisdictions. however, have suffered
because of 'the invasion of the King of Terrors, and as a result many
patient and faithful workers in the great Masonic Vineyard have been
removed from our midst. They have been called,
"Like watch worn and weary sentinels,
To put their armor off and rest in heaven."
Hut yesterday they were with us, holding aloft the banner of Freemasonry; today they are no more, and we do honor unto ourselves by
honoring them in that far off land.
"Like the leaves in the forest when Summer is green,
That host, with their banners, at sunset were seen;
Like the leaves in the forest when Autumn hath blown,
That host, on the morrow, lay wither'd and strown."
