RELA'flONS \.VlTH 01'1-IER JURISDJCTIONS.

I am pleased to advise the Crane! Lodge that our relations with
our sister jurisdictions arc still pleasant, harmonious, and conducive to
the general welfare of the Craft whithcrsoevcr dispersed.
The one aggravating source of friction between Grand Lodges, as
it has been brought home to me, is that of securing reimbursement
from subordinate Lodges of o1 her jurisdictions, for relief extended, or
money advanced to members of such Lodges sojourning within our
midst.
The idea has been advanced on one or two occasions that the
general practice of the fraternity is for each individual Lodge to be
resp~nsible for, and take care of, all Masons within its jurisdiction;
that is to say, of all sojourning nearer that Lodge than any other Lodge,
irrespective of the particular lodge or jurisdiction wherein they hold
th.eir membership. It has occurred to me that such a plan of procedure
will not work out well in practic_e, and that it ought to be discouraged.
If our members leave us and go into foreign lands or j misdictions, we
cannot know or appreciate their actual needs and we must rely to a
great extent upon the investigations and conclusions of those Masons
who may be upon the ground. However. I do not believe that we
should deliberately deliver into someone else's keeping, the sole responsibility of determining the amount of relief or succor which shall be
accorded, together with the degree of worthiness to be attributed, to
;t member of one of our own Lodges.
His individual merits or demerits
which may be known to us alone, will operate in arriving at the amount
of relief of which he should be the recipient. For that reason it is my
belief that the more rational course to pursue is for each subordinate
Lodge to consider itself in duty bound to take care of its own members
wherever they may be, as their necessities may be brought to its atten~ion and as their worthiness may be understood and appreciated, and
111 furtherance of this end that it should regard it as its duty to
reimburse any Loclg-e which may have expended moneys, npon its request
or authorization, for one of its own members.
In addition, T believe that much embarrassment will be saved future
Grand Masters if, by this Grand Lodge, they be authorized to refuse
to enter into correspondence with other Grand Masters for the purpose
of seeking reimbursement for moneys expended, unless some sort of an
~tuthorization has been received by the Lodge asking for reimbursement,
from the Lodge of which the recipient of assistance was a member in~
dicating the character of the relief for which such Lodge would be I1eld
responsible. Tf other jurisdictions refuse to reimburse our si1horclinatc
Lodges for assistance rcnc!crecl to Masons who arc in posses.sion of all
of the evidence which show them entitled to Masonic relief, simply
because the granting of relief was not autiior;;:.-r~(~ ..;y such foreign

GRAND LODG.E OF CALIFORNIA

303

jurisdiction-and I can assure you that that has been the case in
several instances brought to my attention during the past year-then
it would seem to follow as a matter of protection to our own subordinate
Lodges, and as a saving of time and useless effort of future Grand
Masters, that no request for reimbursement should be recognized except in the face of an authorization for the original expendittire.
I inherited from my predecessor a controversy with the Grand
Master of Pennsylvania over the initiation by two of our Lodges of
two petitioners who had theretofore been rejected hy Lodges in Pennsylvania, and over whom Pennsylvania claimed perpetual jurisdiction.
I end~vored to persuade the Grand Master of Pennsylvania that
our Lodges in California had acted in perfect good faith in the matter;
that they were unaware of the claim to perpetual jurisdiction indulged
in by the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, and that, although inquiries
llad been made by them of the Lodges in Pennsylvania which had theretofore rejected the material applying in California, no intimation had
been conveyed of any objections on the part of the Lodges in Pennsylvania, and they had acted on the assumption that no objection
existed.
In addition, I was led to admonish the Grand Master of Penn~ylvania that "the Grand L:::idge of California does not recognize in
any degn.'c at all your claim to perpetual jurisdiction over rejected
candidates applying within the jurisdiction of your Grand LoClge. We
consider a candidate ;vho has resided for at least one year within this
jurisdiction, and who is in good faith a citizen of this State, available
material for membership here, if he possesses the requisite qualifications
in other respects.
"While at all times our Lodges will be most desirous, of course, of
submitting to your Grand Lodge requests for waiver of jurisdiction,
and for information and advice as to the character and standing of
proposed candidates for initiation here who may theretofore have
petitioned in Pennsylvania, nevertheless we decline to be bound or to
recognize the rule of perpetual jurisdiction as contended for by your
Grand Lodge, and I apprehend that it would be unprofitable further to
discuss, either the reasons for, or the righteousness of, our conduct
in so doing."
In spite of the circumstances as above outlined, however, the edict
of the Grand Master of Pennsylvania issued against the Brethren and
they cannot hope for Ma sonic recognition, or the privilege of Masonic
intercourse in Pennsylvania, and I doubt not that that result will
follow in every instance of like character where we initiate a candidate

but against whom objection may be raised by some individual in

It will he a matter of genuine information, I apprehend, to those

1NsPECTORS.

can not commend too highly to the Brethren of the Grand Lodge,
the loyalty aml efticiency of the ]nspectors of the several I\1asonic
Districts in this State. As
whole, and without any noteworthy cxat all. they arc prepared to perform acceptahly the functions

Agreeably to custom in that behalf, near the close of this last
Masonic year, I directed inquiries to the Inspectors of the State concerning matters affecting the welfare of the Craft. as observed by
them in their· several jurisdictions, and I am glad to state that replies
have been received from almost every one of the officers in question.
From these replies I find that almost without exception the Lodges
of the State are being blessed with a due measure of prosperity, and
that, in but very few instances, is the report made that no work has
been had during the past year. One or two, on the contrary, show
by the number of petitions received and degrees conferred that it is
not at all unlikely that they are disposed to believe they are growing

Another Inspector recommends that the Constitution be so amended
as to make it the duty of a Master to declare expelled a member of
his Lodge who has confessed to a commission of a felony in a Court
of Law. Summary punishment appeals to us at times and no doubt
there is considerable efficacy in its infliction. \Ve should, however,
be certain that punishment is due before we adjudge that it shall be
visited upon a given individual. There is as much reason, in the general nature of the case, why the question of the identity of an individual
charged with crime should be ascertained and determined, as the fact
of his having committed the crime itself. I would be fearful that such
a revolution of our method of procedure, even only to the extent specified, might in some instances >vork out an injustice. It might easily
be possible for a Master to he misinformed and to declare expelled
a man who was in truth and in fact not the individual who it was
claimed had confessed in a Court of Law to the commission of a
felony. I am rather impressed with the fact that certainty and surety
in the ad~1inistration of justice, and in the infliction of penalties,
are more to be desired than mere summariness, and that there is no
sufficient reason why an infraction of our Code like the one instanced
should not submit to the due course of procedure in the regular tribunals provided by the wisdom and experience of the fraternity.

CRAKD LODCE. P. & A l\T., OF CALIFORKL\.
January 1, 1915.
To the Subord;inate Lodges, Free and Accepted Masons,
Grand Jurisdiction of California.
BRETHREN: My attention has been called to the fact that the work
of the i\fasonic Employment Bureaus of our State is to a certain
extent hampered, in that insuf~cient attention is given to the matter
of seeming positions, or at least in notifying the Bureaus of possible
openings, in the way of emplovment for worthv and deservitw Brethren
who are in need, not of charity, b~t of work."'
It is obvious to every thinking individual, that the best service
the Fraternity can extend to a worthy Brother :\fason in distress.
consists in practical relief, the securing for such Brother an opportunity to help and better himself; the providing for him of labor and
employment, rather than of money or other purely charitable assistance.
It must be true that, from time to time, among the many different
Lodges in the State, opportunities for employment present themselves,
and it must also be true that, in the event of such an opening, a word·
from a member of such Lodge or from the Master, to the nearest
1\1asonic Employment Bureau would probably result in the filling of
such position by a worthy Mason, and, what is of greater moment and
more importance considering our sworn obligation one to the other,
it would result in the relief of some worthy Brother, eager for work.
and competent to perform the duty required of him. In other words,
around the doors of our :Masonic Bureaus are many Masons who desire, not charity. hut work; known to the fifty-odd thousand of our
brethren, from time to time, arc positions which could be filled bv
these deserving Brethren in distress; our charitable work is onlv hal-f
done if these men and these positions arc not brought togethe-r.
Let each one of us make the effort to put in practice out of the
Lodge those beneficent truths we learn in it, by making a special
effort to keep the Masonic Bureaus advised, from time to time, of
any opportunity for employment in our respective localities, in order
that these opportunitil's may be responded to hy deserving Brethren,
and that the work of the Bureaus may thereby be made more efficient.
I make this appeal with the sincere request that it he considered
carefully and acted upon in the same spirit in which it is sent out,
in order that our work here in the State may assume a more practical and substantial aspect, and that we may be the better enabled
to justify ourselves, ~s wdl as our espousal of the tenets of Urothcrlv
Love. Relief and Truth.
Sincerely and fraternally yours,
(Signed)
BENJAl\IIN F'. BLEDSOE.
Grand Master.

To the Alastcrs, TVardc11s and Brethren,

An unusual amount of conge:stion in the business of the United
States Court here in Los Angeles. aggravated hy the trial of a single
case which has run continuously from about the middle of 1\fay, and
which will probably last for several weeks longer, has made it impossible for your Grand Master to make some official visits he had
planned for this month. l am now hopeful, however, that by using
what may he left of my regular vacation I may he able later to make
some of the visiJs I had in mind.
In this connection I sincerely trust the Fraternity will bear with
me in the' realization that my official duties in my court, because of
the congestion referred to, have borne heavily upon me; in consequence I have felt that I could not, in good conscience, even for the
otherwise laudable purpose of paying Masonic visitations-a ceremony
full of enjoyment for me-neglect or permit to go unperformed the
responsible labors devolving upon my present position.
I recentlv did take an adjournment of my court long enough to
go to San Francisco to participate in the proceedings of "Masonic
Day" at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition. While there I
had the opportunity of observing the great pleasure the larger children
of our home, about forty in number, were deriving from their visit
to the Exposition. Truly they were having the time of their young lives,
and it ought to be a source of real and genuine satisfaction to our
Fraternity that its helpless but deserving wards were thus permitted
this extradrdinary diversion and this great intellectual and educational treat.

This trip of our children from San Gabriel to San Francisco and
return, including a stay of 10 days at the Fair, was made possible because of the initiative and generosity of the Brethren of the following

Such conclusions, of course, are of an extreme nature, but they
illustrate a well known tendency that is valuable more for its display
of mental agility than for its capacity to entertain or inform.

of the time and place duly appointed for their official and ritualistic
promulgation. The course of conduct described and referred to hereinabove meets with my earnest protest and deprecation.

Realizing the demand for "further light in Masonry," I have determined to appoint a Committee on "Masonic Education," and I am
ooing to ask this Committee to formulate such plans for Masonic re~carch and study as will seem to them meet and appropriate. They can
suggest, if they will, Masonic Lectures and Lecturers of real value,
and can doubtless also suggest means and methods whereby the Lodges
generally may become more proficient in the knowledge of the history and destiny of our common institution. I will ask them to render
a report, together with their recommendations to the next Annual
Communication.

I have just directed the Inspectors of this jurisdiction to ascertain and advise me, in their reports upon their several Lodges, as to
the Masonic Charities of our Masonic bodies; are our Lodges maintained merely for the purpose of meeting, conferring degrees, producing Past Masters and displaying the Square and Compass upon
coat lapels and watch chains? Or do they, in addition, recognize and
ever bear in mind that the paramount and controlling and ever-present
obligation resting upon the fraternity has to do with its benevolcnccsassistance to those in distress-service toward our fellowmen?

It was recently brought to my attention by members of a certain
Lodge who had been invited to pay a fraternal visit to another Lodge
in this jurisdiction and assist in the conferring of the Third Degree
therein, that during the progress of the work members of the Lodge
which was the host of th('. occasion, in considerable numbers, remained
out in the social room of the Lodge immediately adjacent to the ante
room, engaged in playing cards.

I am a great believer, of course, in the promotion of the social
features of our Order; it may be an impossibility even to hope to
make a success of our fraternal and benevolent features unless we
at the same time keep in mind, and do that which will tend to promote,
the social fcatnres. One way, of course, of contributing to these social
features is by means of games purely social in their nature and made
use of merely as a diversion. Of these the indulgence in card games,
under the limitations just referred to, may be regarded as not improper. However, it is to my mind highly improper that such card
o-ames should be conducted in the immediate vicinity of the Lodge
;oom during the time of the actual session of a Lodge. If members
must engage in card playing at that particular time they should do it
away from the Lodge room. And I conceive it to be the duty of the
}\.faster of a Lodge, and that he is derelict if he docs not perform it.
to require all members to cease card playing in the social rooms of
the Lodge during the whole of the time that the Lodge may be 111
session.
Tf an initiate observes that some portion of the Lodge membership
takes no more interest in the conferring of the degree upon him than
to make it the occasion and opportunity to beguile the time with a
card game, he will form at once a very unfavorable opinion of our
Order, and an equally unfavorable opinion of men who care no more
for the high principles we teach than to show such open disregard

Frankly, in some Lodges I have visited I have not heard the subject of Masonic Charities mentioned. This circumstance in itself is
inconclusive because there may have been no occasion to mention them
at the precise time of my visit. I do believe, however, that some of
cur Masonic Lodges are, thoughtlessly, paying too little attention to
the subject of Benevolence and that as a matter of fact too little of
our Masonic money is really expended for "relief."
"Brotherly Love" and "Truth" are not the only tenets of Free
Masonry. "Relief" also is included therein, and it was intended that
this tenet should have a practical as well as a ritualistic signification.
The j ing·le of a dollar is the sweetest sound on earth-the most
exquisite music known to man-when it is caused by the expenditure
of money in the alleviation of real distress. Of course "service" in
the cause of humanity does not always imply the use or payment of
mere money. There are many things secured through the operations
of Masonry that money could never buy, no matter how great its
purchasing power might be. This sort of service Masonry is constantly engaged in; the essentially practical means of rendering good to
our fellows, however-the dispensing of tangible, measurable, substantial "relief"-ought to form a regular part of our Masonic routine.
The need is noticeable on every side; we are unmindful of our teachings and unappreciative of our own blessings if we do not heed the
call.
Fra tcrnally and sincerely yours,
(Signed)

BENJAMIN F. BLEDSOE,
Grand Master.

The membership one year ago was 53,179, and notv,·ithstarnling tht•
general cry of hard times and depression of business, we this vear

Last year the suspensions for non-payment of dues amou11ted to 532
and the restoratious 133; this year the suspensions are 732, and the
restorations 146. l cannot escape the conviction that susp'-'nsions arc
not always the result of depressed business conditions, but that in
many instances the member in arrears might he kept in good standing
and Masonic usefulness by studied effort on the part of Masters all(!
Secretaries. The largest Lodge in this jurisdiction, with a memberof more than ni'ne hundred, lost no member last year by reason
of suspension for non-payment of dues. And yet this Lodge pays
annually in the way of relief the princely sum of approximatelv seven
dollars from each member. One of the principal committc~s is a
"Committee on Delinquent l\kmbers," and it is the dutv of the memhers of this committee to ascertain the cause of delinquency-with
the :1appy result that if a member be in distress, his dues arc promptly
re1111ttcd, and if he be negligent merely, he is shown the error of his
ways and his dnty to his fellows. This scheme is hopefully suhmittcrl
tu those L()(lges which lose mcmlwrs by suspension.

BOARD OF RELIEP OF SAN FRA:\CISCO.
To tlzc Ji.'. TV.'. Grand Lodge of California:

The Masonic Board of Relief of the i:ity of San Francisco begs
lea\'(• to present the following report for the year beginning August 25,
1914. and ending August 23, 1915, both dates inclusive:
Owing to the depression in the commercial world, which has been
general all over the country for the past year, and which was greatly
aggravated by the European war, the number of applicants for relief
has greatly increased, but owing to the efficiency of our Employment
Bureau, which works hand in hand with this Board, the amount of relief
given in a great many individual cases was small, and generally only so
much as was necessary to tide the recipient over until work could be
found; consequently, the total amount of relief expe'nded during the
year has been somewhat less than the year previous.
We have been greatly assisted in our work by the following good
brethren of the medical profession, who have always been ready and
willing to respond to any call made on them by this Board, and the
thanks of the fraternity are clue to them:
Doctors Winslow Anderson, H. I. Bloch, ]. C. Egeberg, D. E. F.
Easton, George C. H. Franklin, Otto Freyermuth, A. S. Green, William
P. Read, Jacob Schwarz, E. E. Stone, George A. Wood, Wilhelm
Wal<leyer, and A. W. L. Zillmer.
The matter of relief of dimitted Masons has always been a great
point of contention in the Board and one very hard to act upon.
We are particularly reminded of the case of a brother applying for
relief, presenting a <limit dated March 21, 1890. This man has been,
;1ccording to his own story, located in a great many parts of the country, and had arrived in California five month..> previous to his application,
and under the circumstances he could hardly be considered worthy of

~onsideration after having done nothing for the fraternity for twentytive years; yet the laws of our Grand Lodge distinctly state that the man
is in good standing for six months after his arrival in this State, not
taking into consideration the date of his dimit. Legislation which will
tend to remedy this seeming injustice ought to be had at an early date.

REPORT

L1w Brrno::._.

OF THE .l\JASONlC E.l\lPLOYMENT
OF SAN FRANCISCO.

Secretary.

BURE,\U

The Masonic Employment Bureau of San Francisco takes this opportunity of commending the good work which has been done by the
number of Masons who have taken an active interest and greatly
assisted us in this most important branch of constructive Masonry,
and of expressing to them our sincere gratitude.
Although the past year has been one of tense business conditions,
hy the aid and interest displayed by enthusiastic and consistent friends,
ihe number of positions secured shows an increase of 50 per cent over
last year, and we are proud to record greater accomplishments than
similar bureaus in the larger cities; nor should the good moral effect,
aside from the material aspect, be lost sight of, for making a Brother
self-supporting and self-respecting ought to appeal to every Mason.
We also take this opportunity of thanking the M:. w:. Grand
Master, Benjamin F. Bledsoe, for the timely aid given all the Employment Bureaus in the State by the circular letter addressed to the
various Lodges last January, calling attention to the work of the Employment Bureaus, which greatly assisted us, not only by responses from
the city, hut also by a great many from the country.

from l\Iaster Masons, their widows and children, and positions were
secured as follows:

REPORT OF JURISPRUDENCE CO:\nIITTEE.
Past Grand :\laster Angellotti, Chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence, reported as follows:
To the Af. ·. W. ·. Gra11d Lodge of Cal1fornia:
At the last Communication there was referred to us a question
of the status of a member of one of the subordinate Lodges of this
iurisdiction, who, while rcs:ding within the jurisdiction of Churchi]J
Lodge No. 26 of Fallon, Nevada. was, by the latter Lodge, on conviction therein of unmasonic conduct, suspended from all the rights
and pri,·ilegcs of 1\Iasonry. The N eva<la Lodge certified the record
of the proceedings to our California Lodge. Our Lodge thereupon.
with such record as its only basis and without any trial, entered a
judgment of suspension against the brother. Grand Master Murphey
held, and this l.raml Lodge confirming his ruling also held, that our
Lodge should not have entered any such judgment, for the reason
that if the Nevada Lodge judgment ipso facto operated to deprive
the brother of his Masonic standing here, no judgment of suspension
was essential in our Lodge; and if it did not have that effect. he could
not he deprived of his Masonic standing in this State except by charges
here preferred and a trial thereon.
'Ne expressed no opinion as to whether the Nevada judgment did
have the effect of suspending the brother in this State, and consideration of that question was deferred to this Communication.
It seems very clear to us that in the absence of some provision
of our own law on the subject, the Nevada judgment cannot be given
any effect in California. It is elementary Masonic doctrine that each
l\Tasonic jurisdiction is, within its borders, absolutely supreme and
independent, subject in no way to the constitution, laws or judgments
of any other l.rand Lodge, except in so far as it chooses to make
itself so. \Ve <ln cbim the right to deprive Masons of other jurisdic1illllS rc,;iding in this State of their 1\fasonic standing for umnasonic
c()mluct. lint \\'" cannot claim fnr our judgments in such cases any
extra-territorial effect. Our judgments are operative only within our
n\\·n juri:~dictiou, unless other jurisdictions by positive enactment give

379

At the same time we believe our law should be such that some
effect should be here given to the judgment of another recognized
Masonic j urisdictio:1 that one of our numbers resident therein has been
guilty of unmasonic conduct. With such a judgment before us, the
presumption is that the conclusion of our sister jurisdiction is correct,
and that the brother is guilty of the offense of which he was convicted. In such cases we should at once make investigation as to his
conduct with a view to determining whether he has been guilty of
11nmasonic conduct,, and we should be willing to accept the record of his
conviction elsewhere as pvi111a lac1'c evidence of his guilt of the offense
charged against him. \Ve owe that much not only to the other jurisdiction but also to ourselves. Further we do not cleem it advisable
to legislate at this time.
We therefore recommend the adoption of the follo,ving
AMENDMEN'r ·ro OUR CONsTJTUTJON,

1o \vit:

Amencl section 192 by adding at the end thei;eof the following:
\Vhenever it shall appear by the record of conviction frnm
another Masonic jurisdiction rec()gnized by us that a member
of one of oiu Lodges resident in such jurisdiction has been
suspended or c·xpelled for unmasonic conduct in such jurisdiction while a resident thereof. it shall be the duty of the
Junior Warden of the· Lodge in this jurisdiction of which he
is a member to prefer charges against him for the acts and
conduct alleg~d in the charges preferred in the foreign j urisdiction and of which he was there convicted, and the same proceedings shall thereupon be had as in ordinary cases; provided
that the record of conviction of the foreign jurisdiction shall
be received on the trial as prinia f acie evidence of the guilt of
the brother of such acts ancl conduct.
FRANK MARJON ANGET.LOTTJ,

Past Grand l\faster \Villiam P. Filmer, Vice-President
uf the Masonic Temple Association, presented the followinO' re1)ort which was referred to the Committee on Finance:

'

To THE MosT WoRSHJPfUL GRAND LoDGE oF CALIIIORNL\:
1The Board of Directors of the Masonic Temple Association of California in accordance with its annual custom, presents herewith a full
and c~mplete statement of its financial transactions from the date of
its last report to the Grand Lodge, September 1, 1914, to September
1, 1915.
A complete financial statement of the receipts and expenditures
from September 1, 1908, to September 1. 1914, was presented at the
last communication of the Grand Lodge and is to be found in the Grand
Lodge Proceedings of the year 1914 (see pages 58-65) and is therefore
omitted in our present report.
A study at this time of the financial condition of our Temple reveals
again the urgent necessity of the assistance pledged by the Grand L~dge
in the years that have passed. The promised relief by _the. resolut1~ns
adopted by the Grand Lodge at its last annual commumcation, providing for a bond issue, has proven ineffectual. All Blue Lodges, all
Chapters of Royal Arch Masons, all Councils of Royal and Select Masters, all Commanderies of Knights Templar and all Chapters of Eastern
Star in the jurisdiction of California have been invited and urgec~ to
subscribe for bonds, and to this date but $43,000.00 of an authorized
bond issue of $304,000.00, the approximate present indebtedness, has
been subscribed.
This snm, $43,000.00, is not deemed by the Board of Directors to
he sufficient to warrant the issuance of bonds as contemplated by ~he
resolution and mature reflection since the adoption of the resolution
by the Grand Lodge has caused the Board to decide not to take act~o~1
on the issuance of bonds because our efforts failed to meet the spmt

PHOCI<~EDINGS OF '!'HJ<::

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of the intention of the Grand Lodge. Consultations i.:vere had with
hankers and financiers of San Francisco, who refused to take bonds
because no sinking fund had been provided by the resolution.
Reviewing the records of the past we find that the Grand Lodge
urged the erection of a Temple in San Francisco and promised iL;
"unstinted aid and influence and such financial assistance as its avail~
able resources \vill permit." The erection of a Temple in the central
city of our state has greatly increased interest in the Masonic Order
not only in San Francisco, but throughout the entire jurisdiction. All
the Lodges are benefitting from its existence. It being a Temple f~r all
the Masons of the jurisdiction, all Masons should participate in the
elimination of the indebtedness upon it. This can be accomplished
without increasing the per capita tax, by the Grand Lodge subscribing
for stock in annual installments from its available funds. It was the
policy of the Grand Lodge with regard to the old Temple to invest its
surplus in the stock in the old Temple Association; why should it not
be the policy of the Grand Lodge to invest its money in the new
Temple and reap the benefit from the constantly increasing dividends
and stock value in the years to come? Should the Grand Lodge
purchase the amount of the present indebtedness it will own approximately $578,000.00 of the stock, or considerably over half of the issued
capital stock.
From sentimeut and loyalty to our Order the Grand Commanderv
of Knights Templar, the Grand Chapter of Royal Arch Masons, th~
l\Iasonic bodies of San Francisco are heavy stockholders, and they, with
many small holdings by J\Iasonic bodies, and individual Masons, subscribed largely because the committees who visited those bodies and
urged them to subscribe for stock, represented that the Grand Lodge
was the pmver behind this most important project and was voluntarily
pledged to its financial support and we are strongly of the opinion that
their holdings should be made of value at the earliest possible moment
and this result can ensue only by the liquidation of the indebtedness
upon the Temple.
\Ve invite attention to the fact as shown by the report herewith,
that even during the past year, and with no part of the ground floor
rented, $9058.25 in dividends could have been paid if there had been
no interest charge for money borrowed.
For the information of the representatives of the Grand Lodge,
and to indicate the attitude of the Grand Lodge at the inceptive period
of the Temple and since. \Ve present excerpts from several proceedings.
which not only clearly slin\v that the Crand Loclgc, for several years
before the destructiun of the old 'l\·rnple at Post and :\lontgonwry
,;treets in 1906. desired to !mild a new Temple in Sa11 Francisco and
which also indicate the fact that the Grand Lodge pledged itself to the
ncction nf the present Temple and to the financing thereof. The policy

?.85

of the old Temple Association to invest its surplus funds in the Temple
Association is also shown.
EXCERPTS.
:\f.".W.'. Orrin S. Henderson in 1904 (page.1056) presen.ted a res~­
lution relative to the disposition hy Grand Lodge of its stock m Masomc
I !all Association and the erection of a new Temple. _Referred to

faith of this Grand Lodge is pledged to the ultimate extinguishment

ft may be stated that at the present time no material increase of

which should be determined at once.
The adoption of the plan proposed to the Grand Lodge by the
directors at the last annual communication seems to us to be the best
and most logical plan because:
I. It would be the fulfillment of the obligation both guaranteed
and implied by the Grand Lodge.
2. It will result in rapidly paying off the debts now bearing five
and one-half per cent and six per cent with moneys of the Grand Lodge
which will bring but four per cent in the savings banks.
3. It will result. in six or eight years or at the most ten years, in
dividends to the stockholders.
4. The Grand Lodge will then own the controlling interest in the
Temple Association stock.
It is fully expected that long before ten years shall have passed
the earnings of the Temple will have so increased that they will materially assist in reducing the indebtedness.
From the facts and arguments presented herewith we earnestly
trust that the hrethrC'n of the Grand Lodge will thoroughly realize the
obligations of the Grand Lodge in this most important matter and
that they will adopt some form of resolution that will permanently
finance the Temple and relieve the Temple Association from its present
burden. Under the bonding resolution of last year the $25,000.00
appropriated could not be paid to the Association until the bonds
were issued and was not available for use. \Ve therefore believe
that $50,000.00 should be appropriated this year. That this can be
done from the available resources of the Grand Lodge, without
increasing the present per capita tax, is amply demonstrated by the
Report of the Grand Treasurer, which shows that if this appropriation
is made there will still be a balance more than sufficient to meet all
the annual expenses of the Grand Lodge. We ~uggest the adoption of
the following resolution:
Resolved, That the Grand Lodge subscribe for 25,000 shares of
the capital stock of the Masonic Temple Association of California, to
be paid for as follows: $50,000.00 at this Communication of the Grand
Lodge and $25,000.00 annually hereafter.

fore, Leen prepared for temporary structures, pending the construction

the fireproof buildings are completed. Plans for the permanent structures are now under consideration by your Trustees.

of the Orphans' H'Ome, unless the fifty-cent tax is continued, and as
this is so essential and undoubtedly apparent to every member of the
Grand Lodge, we believe it should be continued.
A most regrettable occurrence of the year to the Board, was the
resignation of our esteemed and much-loved matron, Mrs. H. E. Alexander. Her failing health during the last two years has had a telling effect, and the active duties of caring for our large family became
too great for her strength. Her sweet influence with the children,
and the great respect she commanded from all interested in the Home,
were of inestimable value to the Fraternity. The splendid discipline
and the cheerful spirit of the children stand as a substantial and beautiful monument to her industrious _efforts. The Board, while recognizing that the demands of the position of matron were too heavy for
her, has prevailed upon Mrs. Alexander to accept a position as instructor, which calls for less active responsibilities, and so we shall not
be deprived of her useful influence and personal work with the children.
The selection of a new matron naturally fell to Mrs. M. E. Miller,
the senior in service of our staff at the Home, and during the past year
assistant matron to Mrs. Alexander. Mrs. Miller is most capable in management, economical in all detail, and possesses that unusual faculty of
holding the love of every child without the least suggestion of favoritism. She was Mrs. Alexander's selection as a successor to carry on
the work in which she was so devotedly interested, and the Board was
pleased to endorse her recommendation.

San Francisco, Cal., Sept. 18, 1915.

To the Board of Trustees, Masonic Homes of California.

ELMER E. STONE,
Secretary.

San Francisco, Cal., Sept. 18, 1915.

To the Board of Trustees, Masonic Honies of California.
GENTLEMEN : I have audited the accounts of the Masonic Homes
of California for the year ended July 31, 1915, and following upon ~he
last similar at1dit have presented a complete report thereof, embracmg
statements exhibiting in full details of the financial position and financial operations of the Homes to the date of July 31, 1915.
I have verified the income from reports submitted by the Superintendent, the expenditures by exam.ination of properly approved vouchers, accompanied by supporting invoices or other documents, and the
funds 011 deposit in banks, by examination of bank statements and

purchase of clothing or some sensible necessity. All our boys are uoing well but ·one. who is continually influenced
hy a most determined
and badly misguided parent.
A most satisfactory solntion of the proper housing and caring
for the boys now at work has been reached in the organization of a
cluh. where all the boys can be dormitoried and boarded at the same
place. The boys organized with their own officers, made and executed their own rules, and keep account of their general expense. At
the time of making this report, however, the owner of the property
occupied by the boys met with reverses, and lost the place by foreclosure. The lady leasing the property could not make satisfactory
terms with the new owner, and the boys are temporarily boarding with
private families. The Board will probably secure a suitable place for
the boys soon, that they may be again together, and under the mild but
necessary discipline of a proper and capable person to direct their care
and organization.
The children at the Home are deeply appreciative of the care they
receive, and through the influence of their instrnctors are striving to
show their gratitude by a substantial improvement in all the duties
assigned to them. Their special teachers in music, dancing, drilling and
manual work, compliment them upon their unusual application and persistency of effort. Their school work is marked by an equal interest,
and is evidenced by the fact that of fifty-eight pupils from the Home.
only two failed to make their grade, and one of these was a new boy
who was confosed in his classes hy a transfer from a school graded
differently.

We continue to arrange evenings of entertainment through committees supplying varied programs. Many clever and original numbers
are arranged that would reflect credit on older persons. All patriotic
and other holidays arc observed with an appropriate program. Visitations of the Board of Relief, Past Masters' Association, Lodges coming
in a body, etc., are always given a short program, that the Fraternity
may know to some extent the care given the children,
The greatest care is exercised in the selection of the women who
are given the responsibility of training the young minds and hearts of
those left for the Fraternity to bring up to a high standard of citizenship. Due credit must be given those who give many hours a day in
their respective duties to the special advancement of the personality
and culture of the individual child. The new child brought to the
Home has been a victim of reverses, and, in many cases, a long time
without care and training. :i\foch patience is required to overcome
some of these unfavorable conditions. The general system, however,
of all working to one end soon obtains results.

l'HOCEBDlNGS OF THE

l\Iiss Dorothy Lyndall continues her splendid and valuable work
teaching special dances. Our girls delight in this work and respond
well to l\Iiss Lyndall's skillful training. l\Iiss Lyndall 1s devoted to
the work and accepts no compensation.
Mrs. Lela Buckman has splendid results in her piano instruction,
though her advanced pupils nearly always leave the Home at a most
unsafr;factory period of her work. Her musicales, given at the end
of each term, always show splendid advancement.
The notable e\·ent of the year, and one that will mark one of the
brightest spots in their entire lives. is the visit of the older children
to the Exposition at San Francisco, as the guests of the Lodges of the
Bay Cities. Everything was provided to make the trip both instructive
and cnj oyable. Guides were furnished and a systematic arrangement
nf the trips was so made that the best features were 1'iven suitable
attention. Bro. Leo Bruck devoted much attention and has won the
enrlasting friendship of the children. His thoughtfulness in all
matters of arrangement. his ability in securing concessions, and his
generous yet economical handling of funds, marks him as a past
master in this work. Bro. Mitchel was tireless in looking after the
children, and Mrs. Herndon, of the Board of Relief, endeared herself
to tbcm hy lier continuous assistance. Bro. John Whicher. T. J.
·Baker, \V. A. Sherman and Harry Johnson always had something new
for them, and in our list of Donation° is shown the many kindnesses
extended by the generous l\Iasons and Eastern Star members of San
Francisco.
All the children were taken to the Camp at Balboa, where the usual
courtesies were extended, and a happy, hearty and healthful vacation
was enjoyed. Of sixty-six children in camp. only seven did not learn
to swim. Side trips were arranged to neighboring beaches and all
local pleasures indulged in. Jn swimming contests with a similar camp
of boys of a military school, our boys won nearly all the events.
Our health record still remains practically perfect. N" o serious
illness has at any time ,·isited the Home. Dr. Dunsmoor. the good
guardian of our health, is as faithful as ever in caring for all our little
troubles physically and particularly in arranging suitable diet and forms
of exercise.
The children have a new and most generous and faithful friend
in Bro. Paul 0. Paulsen of Silver Trowel Lodge. This generous Lodge,
always thoughtful of the children, excelled itself and all other Lodges
for individual gifts, in presenting the Home with a splendid moving
picture machine, with all necessary equipment, screen, roller cases,
wiring, etc. But they gave us more when they gave us Bro. Paulsen,
who goes to all the agencies, selects the most suitable films, and comes

March 14-Through the kindness of Mrs. E. W. Brooks of Pasadena, the First Regiment Band of forty-six pieces gave the children a
most delightful concert on the Home grounds. The band was liberal
in their numbers and played many selections wanted as favorites by the
children.
1\farch 31-Southland Chapter, 0. E. S., of Pasadena took the
children auto riding, picture show and good supper in Pasadena. An
annual affair.
April 11-Visit of several members of Silver Trowel Lodge. A
good program rendered.
April 29-Ladies of Highland Park Chapter No. 263, 0. E. S.,
visited the Home. The children entertained the guests, then disposed
of their generous supply of home-made candies.

June 22 to July 2-The visit of the children to the Exposition at
. July 5~Pasadena Commandery devoted a day of sport and games
with the children. They brought their ladies along, who provided a
fine lunch on the lawn, in which the children participated.
July 9 to August 25-Trip to Camp Collins at Balboa.
August 5-Bro. Wm. Schneider visited the children in camp.
Brought with him a fine, thick fillet mignon for each member of the
camp, barbecue irons, French rolls, chili and heans, and all necessarv
appointments for a barbecue. He then donned his "chef" uniform and
gave the children a fine treat.
August 22-Dr. J. M. Dunsmoor and family called at camp. The
children gave them boat rides and made them feel at home. He then
left them a good supply of candy, which almost brought him back
professionally.
August 30--The Shrine Club of Long Beach gave the children their
annual "Melonfest'' at the ranch of Bro. J. D. Humiston, near Azusa.
The melon crop was reduced in liberal proportions.

I wish to extend my appreciation of the services rendered by the
Matrons throughout the year in their respective departments.
I take occasion to express to the Board of Trustees my sincere
gratitude for the friendly advice and substantial support which at all
times I have received at their hands.
Respectfully,
FRANK

B. HARTMAN,
Superintendent.

Brother John H. Bean introduced the following proposed
amendment to the Uniform Code of By-Laws:
Resolved, That section 2, article V, of the Uniform Code of ByLaws, relating to Treasurer. be amended by striking out the words
"if required by the Lodge," so that the section shall read as follows:
"Sec. 2. He shall execute a good and sufficient hond to the Master
for the faithful performance of his duties." ·

Rcsoh•cd, That section 2 of article VI of the lJniform Code of
By-Laws, relating to Secretary, be amended by striking out the words
"if required by the Lodge," so that the section shall read as follows:
"Sec. 2. He shall receive such compensation for his services as the
Lodge may direct; and he shall execute a good and suificicnt hond
to the Master for the faithful performance of his duties."

This was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence,
who reported back verbally to the effect that the proposed
amendment was a matter of policy for the Grand Lodge to
decide. The resolutions were laid over until \Vednesday
morning, when, after consideration, they were voted upon
and defeated.

Brother S. H. Kent, Past Master of Golden Gate Lodge
X o. 30, introduced the following:
Resohicd, That the dues of any brother of any Masonic Lodge
in the State of California, who has been in good standing for fortyfive years, may be remitted for the balance of his life, by a majority
vote of the members present at any annual meeting of the Lodge of
which he may be a member.

The above was referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, who subsequently brought in the following report
thereon:
The proposed resolution is in violation of section 128 of the Conwhich forbids the remission of dues for any stated period in
advance; and we therefore recommend that it be not adopted.

431

Also by Brother Kent:
Resolved, That the Grand Lodge adopt a form and style of Past
Master's jewel, to be made of· gold and without any setting of diamonds, to cost not to exceed twenty-five dollars, and that retiring
.:\Tasters he presented with such jewel, the funds for the purchase
thereof to be taken from the Lodge treasury.

The Committee on J urispruclence, to which was referred
the resolution, reported that
Our Grand Lodge has been opposed to the use of Lodge funds
for any such purpo;.;e since its Communication of 1853, and we therefore recommend that the resolution be not adopter!.

The recommendation was indorsed by Grand Lodge.

Brother Kent also presented a resolution to amend section 128 of the Constitution by providing that a retiring
Master shall be presented with a certificate of life membership and forbidding a collection from the members for gifts
or presents of any kind; and also providing for a collection
for the relief of a member in distress when the Lodge is
not financially able to relieve him. It was referred to the
Committee on Jurisprudence, who reported back as follows:
Gnder section 129 of the Constitution, the only way in which a
certificate of life membership can he presented to the retiring Master
is by purchasing it. Our law requires that the life membership fund
shall be forever kept, and the income thereof alone used. Section
88a forbids the use of the funds to purchase presents for retiring
officers or for distinguished brethren, and this has been our law since
1853. We are not inclined to recommend any legislation to prevent
members of the Lodge from voluntarily subscribing to a fund to be used
for the presentation of a testimonial to the retiring Master, as we
think the members of the Lodge can well control such a matter.

~titution,

Our present law makes it obligatory on our Lodges to relieve
their members, and there is now ample power to make any collection
necessary for the relief of distress.

Grand Lodge concurred in the recommendation, and the
resolution was lost.

\Ve the re fore recommend that the proposed amendments to section 128 be not adopted.

The recommendation of the Committee was adopted.

There was presented in behalf of brethren living at Fort
1\ rcDowell, Angel Island, the following:
The brethren on Angel Island are desirous of organizing a new
Lodge of Masons, and all of them belonging to the army, they desire
to be enabled to draw members from the various army posts around.
the bay. They do not ask for exclusive jurisdiction for posts other
than 1\ngel Island, but the right to work in conjunction with those
of San Francisco and .:\Iarin counties. There are approximately
thirty ;\laster Masons residing at this time on the island.

The minutes of yesterday's sessions were read and
approved.

Our Constitution now permits the application of a person belonging to the army or navy to be received by dispensation, although he
may not have the qualilication of residence in the State required of
others. (Section 96, Constitution.) In 1912 the Grand Lodge adopted
section 92A, which provides a• procedure for changing the jurisdiction
of Lodges, and your Committee feels that it would be unwise to recommend any change in our law at this time.

To the Jf.". W.". Grand Lodge of California:

The Grand Lodge was then railed off until 10 o'clock
\\' ednesday morning.

Your Committee on Returns begs to report as follows:
The reports returned to the V.". W.". Grand Secretary show that
the year just passed has been marked by a steady and substantial
progress both in the total membership in the jurisdiction an<l also in
the income of the Grand Lodge from its subordinate Lodges. There
has been a net gain of 2162 members. and a net increase in the payments to the Grand Lodge from the subordinate Lodges of $1.756.85.
The retnrns also show a decrease of 128 in the nnmhcr who have
dimitted; and an increase of 13 in the number who ha\'e restored
themselves to good standing over the figures for 1914. But we regret
that there is an increase of 210 in the number of brothers suspended
for non-payment of dues. Steps should he taken at once to rednce this
number, for based on the returns of the last two years, only about
one-seventh of those who ha\·e been suspended ever are restored to
membership and so six-sevenths of the number suspended represent a
net loss to the Order.

As ;i

each year, anrl it is absolutely essential tbat we erect a "large, nc\~·

You will appreciate, of course, that a tax of $2.40 on each .'.\Iason
in California is not felt by each indi,·idual member of the Order, as

sufficiently depletes the treasury of each Lodge to make it necessary
that something be done to materially reduce the great burden of taxation now borne by our constituent Lodges. The question is, How can
this he accomplished?
\V c cannot reduce the expense of the Grand Lodge, and the annual
per capita tax of 50 cents for the erection of buildings will be necessary
for a few years, or until such time as we have fully complied with the
requirements of the Grand Lodge, in building proper structures for the
protection of our charges.
\Vhereforc. tl1c most feasible plan for taking care of the annual
fund, and e\·cry .'.\[ason in California can help this fund. This can be
accomplished. not l1y the immediate contribution of cash, though that
would be much appreciatcrl, hut by the preparation of your will, remembering the l\Iasonic Hom cs of California with such amount as you can
afford, having consideration. of course, for your own family, also.
Every man. and particularly C\'Cry Mason, should prepare his will
so that if accident or illness overtake him proper disposition can be
made of his property. in accordance with his own desires. It is
therefore hoped that if our members have drawn their wills, or may
do so in the immediate future, some provision will be made, no matter
how small the bequest may be. for the :MASONIC HOMES OF
CALIFORNIA. which 1s the corporate title of our great .'.\Iasonic

. \side from the comments made by us under the captions of the
various J nrisdictions rcportC'd on herein, we have only a frw observations to make concerning one or two matters which ha vc come to th'·
attention of practically all of the Jurisdictions within the past year.
REQUEST FOR RECOGNITION OF GRANDE LOGE
NATIONALE, ETC., OF FRANCE.

Thi,.; request was before our Grand Lodge at its Annual Communication a year ago. Action thereon was deferred until fuller information could be obtained concerning this alleged Grand Lodge.
This request for recognition was addressed about a year ago to
prohably e\·cry Grand Lodge of Masons in the world, because in our
reading we have encountered it everywhere. Recognition has been
accorded by a few Grand Bodies and we are very certain that the
few instances where recognition has been extended was because
of hasty action, without sufficient inquiry as to the existence, or
non-existence, of underlying requirements for recognition, and based.
we presume, in every case upon the assertion that recognition had
been extended by the Grand Lodges of England and Scotland.
Because Craft Masonry traces its origin, ;is a rule, to the Grand
Lodge of England is no reason why greater weight should attach to
the action of England in extending recognition than would attach to
recognition extended by some other Grand Lodge. In fact, England
and Scotland are at the present time, in many ways, unsafe guides
to follow in the matter of recognition. Recognition by these Grand
Bodies is frequently based upon selfish and narrow considerations, ;is
is shown in the refusal of these Grand Bodies to recognize certain
Grnnd Lodges that have been formed in Australia, New Zealand, and
other places, because this action will affect these Grand Lodges
adversely, from a purely selfish standpoint; and. while recognition
has in the cases of most of the Australian and the New Zealand Grand
Lodges been grudgingly extended, this has not heen done until practically all of the rest of the Masonic world had freely received into the
family of Grand Lodges these sovereign bodies; yet, even now England
and Scotland refuse to grant recognition to the Grand Lodge of
Queensland, a Grand Lodge that has received recognition from nearly
every other Grand Lodge on earth.
For these reasons, therefore, the recognition, or non-recognition,
by England or Scotland, of another Grand Lodge is not by any means
conclusive as to the status of that Grand Lodge, and vastly greater
weight is to be attached to the action of such Grand I,odges in our
own country as :'\1assachusetts, or Wisconsin, or Pennsylvania, that
arc guided hy the counsels of careful and conservative Masonic
scholars.

It, of course, is inevitable that we, as l\fasons, should feel the
profoundest sympathy and sorrow for the a wfol distress occasioned
by the unprecedented conflict in Europe, and this sorrow and griei
extends not only to Masons who are suffering from the conflict, but to
all of the innocent victims of this causeless war, wherever located and
whether they be Masons or not. It is doubtful, in our judgment, however, whether the victims of the war in Europe of Masonic affiliation
arc at this time proper subjects for consideration in the disbursement
of Masonic charity. Our efforts in this direction would be as a grain
of sand on the seashore, and the distress caused by this awful war
must be alleviated and taken care of, not hy such organizations as
the l\fasonic Fraternit¥, but by the Governments of Europe themselves.
After the conflict is over it may then be proper to consider to
what extent and how l\fasonic charity may be extended.

the annual meeting held on February 22 of each year at Alexandria,

This indtation to JOll1 in the movement was declined, as were
two similar invitations received by this Jurisdiction in previous years.
Personally, we are in sympathy with the action taken by Arkansas,
not because of any lack of appreciation of the grandeur of the character
of \Vashington or of his influence upon Masonry, but because these
annual gatherings of representatives from different Grand Bodies hold
the germs of a danger that the creation of a General Grand Lodge
of the United States may be attempted, and this is the same objection,
also, that we have to the so-called Annual Conference of Grand
Masters.
Of the seven or
conferences of this character that have thus
far been held, we believe it may be said that not one has concluded
its sessions without the introduction by someone of a resolution looking
to the creation of a General Grand Lodge, and, while these resolutions
have always been frowned upon and voted down, nevertheless the
thought is always latent, and there are always certain individuals who
are attempting to eommit these annual conferences to the idea of a
General Grand Lodge, which is antagonistic to the spirit of our
Institution; yet, as stated, the attempt to "modernize" Masonry and to
put it into the class of fraternal organizations of recent origin, is
constantly being made at these annual gatherings.

and in rendering opinions and decisions upon qncslions of law and

One of his dcci:<ions was to the effect that a Lodge acquires
exclusive jurisdiction over a petitioner, whose petition lawfully proceeds
to a ballot. In case of his rej<:ction such exclusive jurisdiction
terminates ;1t the end of one year. In case of his election such exclusive
jurisdiction becomes perpetual. He held that the exclusive jurisdiction
of a Lodge under a foreign Grand Jurisdiction will be recognized as
being equal hut not superior to the exclusive jurisdiction of one of l1is
own Lodges under like circumstanc<'s.
The Jurisprudence Committee agreed with this decision, so far
as it pertained to an elective petitioner, but held that in regard to
rejected material the Grand Lodge has always claimed jurisdiction over
all material living within its confines, which includes rejected applicants
as well as the profane, and requires a Masonic residence of six months
to enable the petitioner to seek admission in the Lodge having jurisdiction over his residence.
In like manner jurisdiction is rekascd as soon as said material
ceases to bt: a resident of the Grand Jnriscliction.
The Report of the Jurisprudence Committee. which is undoubtedly
correct, was sustained by the Grand Lodge.

His report is an excellent docmnent; he presents in a clear and

He makes a long quotation from the address of Grand Master

In his introduction, he makes note of certain outstanding features
which he has observed in connection with his recent examination of
Grand Lodge Proceedings. He finds that there is a growing sentiment
in all of the Jurisdictions in favor of more extended efforts along
certain lines; for instance, efforts to promote the study side of
Masonry by lectures given by well-informed brethren and by the
reading of books, Masonic publications, etc.; a tendency to develop the
social side in individual Lodges for the benefit not only of the
members but of their families; a tendency to expand the charitable
side of the organization either by building Masonic Homes or by
increasing benevolent funds. He finds a tendency to relax the rigor
heretofore exercised by certain Jurisdictions against those not physically perfect and refers with approval upon this subject to the action
taken in Indiana in 1911, by an amendment to the Constitution which
provided that the Grand Master may, with the consent of the Committee
on Jurisprudence, allow Lodges to receive and ballot on petitions for
membership of those who can, by the aid of artificial appliances, conform
to the ceremonies of the Order. Keeping all of these things in mind,
he adds that it is not surprising that we hesitate to bar the door of
Masonry to the lofty mind and the great heart, who may be fully
equipped to do the big things for our Fraternity, for the reason alone
that misfortune may have placed upon him some physical defect.
We believe that Brother Gay is absolutely right, because we have
ceased to be operative Masons and are speculative Masons only, and it
should be the inward qualifications and not the outward qualifications
that should be a matter of scrutiny, and if a man's character can pass
muster, very little attention should be paid to mere physical defect.
Brother Gay has embodied in his report an exceedingly valuable
statistical table pertaining to Masonic Homes. The table was prepared
by Brother C. A. Bridwell, President of the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Orphans' Home of Arkansas.

Upon the subject of physical defects, the Grand Master observes
a tendency in most of our Jurisdictions to relax the rigid rule demanding physical perfection. \Ve are in accord with him in his views and
take pleasure in quoting him upon the subject, as follows:
"A spirit of liberality is now recognized in some Jurisdictions,
where there is offered a little elasticity, in the general restrictions of
our Order as to the physically disqnalified petitioner. There is a
teaching in the higher level to which Masonry lifts men where physical
defects are forgotten, and only moral character and a general ability
to be useful is measured. The tendency of this age is toward a
broader and more charitable plane.
"I do not recommend the repeal ot our present laws governmg
this subject, but I do firmly believe that this Grand Lodge could, with
advantage and perfect safety, show leniency where the disqualification
is not absolute, and amend these laws so as to partially relax our
present ironclad requirements, by adding thereto, a right vested only
in the Grand Master; giving him the privilege to make a thorough and
personal investigation, with the power to recommend the applicant,
if in his sound judgment, the proposed postulant was generally regarded
by the brethren of his community, as worthy to partake of the privileges
of the Fraternity."

Application was made to the Grand Lodge of Kentucky, the same
as to other Grand Lodges, for contributions to relieve the distress
incident to the war now raging on the continent of Europe. ' The
Grand Master expressed the opinion, in which we concur, that, as
patriotic people, it is incumbent upon us to avoid any zealous efforts that
may lead our government into unncutral conduct and that by bestowing
undue favors in certain dir<.>ctions offense might be given in other
directions, and it is no lack of humanity to say that, while the Masons
of this country would undoubtedly he glad to as'dst in laudable measures
of relief, yet the misery incident to war upon such a gigantic scale as
is now raging is so overwhelming and widespr<.>ad that the puny efforts
that we might put forth to relieve Masonic distress would be as a
grain of sand upon the seashore toward ameliorating the appalling conditions, and, in our judgment. abont the only logical method of J\fasonry
contributing to the relief of the distressful conditions in Europe is
contributions to such organizations as the Red Cross.
The Grand Master, we are surprised to say, recommended that
the Grand Lodge adopt a cipher ritual, the alleged purpose of which
was to render the "work'' uniform. Not only did the Grand }faster
recommend the adoption of a cipher, but the CQmmittec to which it
was referred approved the Grand Master's recommendation, but both
the Grand Master and the committee \Vere happily turned down hy the
Grand Lodge.
Personally, W<.> have never heen able to understand how anv cipher
can be adopted which docs not infringe the E. A. obligation. The secrets of Masonry, we are early taught, are confided to the
repository of faithful breasts and are communicated from "mouth to
ear," and are in this way passed from generation to generation, and, in
our opinion, it is in no wise essential to the true spirit of Freemasonry
that there should be absolute uniformity of language and that the
letter-perfect recital is necessary in order that the trne realization of
the hidden and deeper meanings of J\fasonry may be realized.

One of the grand things about Masonry is that, while each J urisdiction is within itself sm·ercign and ~uprcme, and while different J nrisdictions will differ as to the precise language oi the unwritten work,
yet the landmarks and principles arc c1·crywhcrc the same, with the
result that a Mason who is truly a :Mason has no diffirnlty in proving
himself as such in Jurisdictions other than the one to which he belongs,
notwithstanding, as stated, there arc wide variations in the language
of the unwritten work.
Ciphers or keys, while they have at different times been authorized
in a few Jurisdictions. have, we believe, almost invariably in the end
been condemned by those Jurisdictions and destroyed.

Most Worshipful Brother William W. Clarke is the author of
another excellent Report on the Proceedings of Grand Lodges.
California, 1913, receives generous recognition, with liberal quotations from Grand Master filmer's Address and Brother Hervey's
Oration.
In his "Conclusion," Brother Clarke averts to the centralizing
tendencies of the present time, and indicates in clear and forceful
language his observation to the effect that Grand Lodges, which arc
in fact the creations of Subordinate Lodges, have usurped powers to
such an extent that initiative has practically been withdrawn from
Subordinate Lodges, which are controlled almost as automatons by
the Central Body, and he observes that this spirit of centralization is
still in progress and that the latest manifestations of it are insidious
efforts which seem to be working in certain directions toward the
creation of a General Grand Lodge, and he wonders if these Annual
Grand Masters' Conferences may not indeed be a part of propaganda
to bring Masonic bodies under the control of one supreme authority.

He calls attention to the fact that only a few years ago a Grand
Master of Indiana openly advocated, and we may say he is still openly
advocating, a Central Masonic Authority, and mentions that the Grand
Master of Oregon plainly asked other Jurisdictions to unite with it in
the organization of a Central Grand Lodge.
Brother Clarke's observations along these lines are certainly worthy
of careful perusal.

Our Pennsylvania friends take issue with this statement and
stoutly maintain that Marnnry in this country first had a footing in
that commonwealth.
Possibly the difference of op1mon might be reconciled upon the
basis that Masonry in both Massachusetts and Pennsylvania existecl
before the formation of the English Grand Lodge in 1717 and possibly
has just as valid a right to be considered "regular" as did the
individual Lodges in England before they came together and formed
a Grand Lodge.

A distinguished visitor, in the person of Most Worshipful Alfred
\V. Cheesman, Grand :!\faster of Louisiana, was received, after which
the Grand Master delivered his Annual Address.

vVe quote from the opening of his Address as follows:
''\Ve are assembled in this, the most historic city of our grand old
State, and have been welcomed by brethren whose untiring efforts in
the cause of Masonry call for our cordial admiration. How pleasant it
is to again meet and exchange friendly greetings after the year's labor
is done, and how reassuring and delightful to know that these reunions
are not for an hour or a day, but will occur again and again as the
years cycle by, while we, like pilgrims, plod along the rugged road of
life. Like the strings of an instrument touched by a skillful hand, each
string producing its own peculiar tone, yet all blending in one sweet
melodious harmony, so as ,\fasons, as diverse in character and feelings
as in language and complexions, yet all united in one common object, to
benefit mankind, all pressing forward to one common goal-Eternity.
"In this purpose we have been permitted to continue on our peaceful
way while many of our sister Jurisdictions are in the throes of war, torn
asunder by the savage force of armed invasion, and without any discussion of the causes, impulses or ambitions involving in a death
struggle most of the greatest countries of the earth-those with whom
we enjoy the closest bonds of fraternal intercourse, let us at least do
our utmost to relieve the suffering of those afflicted and pray for the
ultimate attainment of universal peace."

Fortunately, the Grand Master was enabled to travel extensively
throughout the State and pay fraternal and official visits to many of
the Subordinate Lodges of the Jurisdiction.
Seven Lodges which had received charters at the preceding Annual
Communication were duly constituted; four dispensations were issued
to form new Lodges; numerous Emergent Communications were held
for the purpose of placing cornerstones of public buildings.
Of the numerous rulings made by him within the year, only two
were considered of sufficient importance to warrant a so-called "decision." One of the questions was whether a Lodge in this Jurisdiction
could entertain an application for membership based on a <limit issued
by a Lodge within the Jurisdiction of New Jersey. The Grand Master
decided the question in the affirmative, and the only thing about the
case that renders it significant is the fact that Mississippi and New
Jersey are not in fraternal relations with each other, Mississippi having
suspended relations because in the Jurisdiction of New Jersey there is
a regular chartered Lodge of negro Masons.

95th Annual, Portland, May 5, 6, 7.
Lodges, 203; members, 30,294; gain, 422.
There were present sc\'entcen Grand Officers, nine Past Grand
l\Iastcrs, and reprcscntati\'Cs of 188 of the 203 chartered Lodges.
l n his Address, the Crane! ::\[aster feelingly refers to the death
within the year of Very \Vorshipful "Willard F. Hicks, Grand Treasurer.
The Grand l\Iastcr gives expression to the admonition, so frequently encountered in Grand Masters' Addresses, touching the necessity of the exercise of great care in the selection of members to the
encl that unfit material may not he received.
Masonry is not a reformatory institution and only "good men and
trne'' arc supposed to be taken within its folds.
A notable event of local interest occurred in a presentation by
the Grand Master of a silver lo\·ing cup to Brother Stephen Barry,
Grand Secretary, as a mark of appreciation of his ser\'icc of 58 years
in the Grand Secretary's office, first for a period of 35 years as
assistant to his father, who for many years served as Grand Secretary,
and for 23 years as Grand Secretary himself. This record of 58
years of continuous se~vicc as a Grand Lodge officer is certainly
remarkable, and probably a world record.
The Grand Master submitted eleven decisions on points of J\Iasonic
law. The Committee on Jurisprudence requested that they be given
until the next Annual Communication to report on the same.
One of the rulings reported by the Grand Master was to the
effect that charges may be preferred by one who stands suspended
from membership for non-payment of dues.
In our j udgmcnt it is questionable if this decision is upheld by
the Committee on J urisprudencc, for it is difficult to understand how
one who has been suspended from all the rights and prh·ileges of
Masonry can prefer charges against a Mason in good standing any
more than could an expelled Mason or a profane.
Another decision which seems to us at least peculiar was to the
effect that a Lodge could not confer the degrees upon a candidate of
another Lodge. The rule that is now almost universal (Pennsylvania
being the only State, we believe, now remaining holding an opposite
opinion) is that degrees may, as a matter of courtesy, be conferred

REPORT ON CORRESPONDEXCE.
68

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

by one Lodge upon the request of and for the benefit of another
Lodge.
The Grand 1Iastcr also ruled th;it an appropriation could not be
made from the fonds of the Lodge for the purchase of a jewel to be
presented to the retiring :\faster. Technically, possibly, this decision
may be correct, but \\C kno\\' that it is the well-nigh universal
practice of Lodges to make appropriations of this character, and
there is in principle no reason why the Lodge should not be permitted
to express its appreciation for one who has devoted perhaps years of
unselfish effort for the advancement of the cause of Masonry and the
promotion of the welfare of his own Lodge.
In closing his "°'1Jldrcss, the Grand Master quotes the eulogy of
:\[asonry, by Brother Charles W. Moore, of whom the late Past Grand
1Iaster Drummond of this Jurisdiction said that, in his day and
generation, there was no more correct expositor of the Masonic law
on this continent than :\Ioore, as follows:

":\Iasonry is indeed an universal institution. History docs not
furnish a parallel. Tt exists where Christianity has not gone; and its
claims \\'ill he respected even where the superior claims of religion
would fail. It is ne1·cr obscured by the darkness of night. The eye
of day is always upon it. Its footprints are to be traced in the most
distant regions and in the remotest ages of the earth. Among all
civilized peoples, and in all Christianized bnds, its existence is recognized. Un;iffccted by the tempests of war, the storms of persecution,
or the denunciations of fanaticism, it still stands proudly erect in the
sunshine and clear light of Heaven, with not a marble fractured, not
a pillar fallen. Tt still stands, like some patriarchal monarch of the
forest. with its vigorous roots riveted to the soil, and its broad limbs
spread in broad outline against the sky; and in generations yet to come,
as in ages past, the sunlight of !wnor and renown will delight to linger
and play amid its venerable branches. And if ever, in the Providence of
God, lashed by the storm and riven by the lightning, it shall totter
to its fall, around its trunk will the ivy of filial affection, that has so
long clasped it. still cling, and mantle with greenness and verdure its
ruin and decay."

arc. no douht, cnjoyahlc to those permitted to participate therein.
There is, we believe, invariably, at these Annual Conferences. a resolution
introduced looking to the formation oi a General Grand Lodge. and
at each conference thus far these resolutions arc indignantly repudiated.
with the accompanying declaration that nothing is intended along these
lines. In fact, these denials have become so emphatic and frequent
that an observer is almost constrained to ·say, with the poet, "Methinks
she doth protest too much.''
One of ·the alleged purposes of these Conferences, at least the one
that is most persistently advanced, is the idea of securing uniformity
in the "work" throughout the various Jurisdictions, as well as uniformity touching such questions as "penal jurisdiction," etc.

Tt is our belief that these very differences, which these Solons
complain of, constitute one of the distinctive features of Freemasonry
that differentiates our Institution from modern imitators, and, while
these immaterial variations exist, and must exist if each Grand Lodge
is sovereign and independent, yet there is an umlerlying agreement and
harmonv in the great essentials which are common to Masonry throughont th~ world, and the fact that the "work" of Pennsylvania, for
instance, may differ materially from the "work" of California, yet
California Ma sons and Pennsylvania :\fasons have no difficulty in
proving to each other that they are all members of the same great
Fraternity.
One of the outstanding features uf \lis-onri i\brnnry is ib magniticcnt :VIasonic Home. The matter of providing an increased income
to meet the increased dcmarnls upon the Iiome came before the Grand
Lodge for its serious consideration, and several plans for the creation
of a permanent Endowment Fnnd for the Masonic Home were sug-

The Report of the Committee on Recognition of Foreign Grand
Lodges recommended the recognition of the ::-Jatioual and Independent
Grand Lodge of France and her Colonies, alleging as a reason for this
that England and Scotland have recognized the new claimant. It is
not always safe to base action in matters of this kind upon what
England or Scotland may do; and. as a matter of fact, it was pointed
out by Brother Gallagher of Massachusetts that England had probably
not recognized this Body at all; that its chief officer had been a
member of the Grand Orient of France; that the new Body does not
consist of more than two or three Lodges, with a total membership of
perhaps less than seventy.

If Brother Gallagher is not mistaken in his deductions, and he
usually is very accurate, this so-called new Grand Lodge possesses small
grounds for asking recognition as a sovereign Grand Lodge of Craft
Masonry from the other Grand Lodges of the world.
The Grand Master's suggestion that the ..:\merican Flag be made
a part of the Lodge furniture met the approval of the Grand Lodge.

C. C. Woods. In his Introduction he refers, am~ng other things, to
the subject of "Advertising Our Order," very properly, in our opinion,
taking a strong position against anything along these lines. He speaks
particularly of the permission so often asked for by Lodges in certain
Jurisdictions of attending church in regalia, and while he is himself a
minister he objects seriously to this as an infraction of good taste.
Freemasonry, he truthfully avers, does not need any advertising
methods to advance its standard. It is above all of these modern
methods of attracting attention.
In his report for the current year now before us. he reviews

As is the usual custom in this J uriscliction, immediately after the
opening exercises of the Grand Lodge, the Body adjourned to listen to
the Annual Sermon, which, in this instance, was preached by the
Grand Chaplain, William Dri ffilcl. This may be all right in Nova
Scotia; it probably is; in fact, in nearly all oi the Canadian J urisclictions
it is an ordinary occurrence for Lodges to attend church in reg·alia,
and, therefore, it does not seem particularly out of place for the Grand
Lodge to adjourn after the formal opening to listen to a sermon from
a member of the clergy of the High Church of England; yet, :Masonry
is supposed to assemble upon its broad pbtform the members of all
creeds and denominations, the only religious requirement being belief
in the Supreme Being, and, to our mind, then: is a distinct impropriety
in expecting Masons of the Hebrew faith. for instance, to attend a
Church of England service; and it is difficult, also, to banish the
thought that the purpose of these chmch services is not so much a
sincere desire to praise God as through pomp and ceremony, to be
seen and admired of men.
Notwithstanding slight differences of o•Jmion which we may hold
