The :\.Iasonic Home estallli:ohmcnt. for instance, at Elizabethtown,
while still almost in its infancv is n·t in its proportions the most
magnificent institution of the ki~~l on .earth.

In speaking of the Masonic .Home, it . perhaps, is more modern
than any similar cstablishmcnt in our country, awl the primary thought
appears to be in the establishment of the Homes at Elizabethtown to
get away from the "institutional" or "inmat~" idea. This idea, according to our friends in Pennsylvania, is out uf date and antiquated, and
the system which this great Jurisdiction is establishing is the cottage
system, the co1nmunity system, the system which shall carrv out to
its fullest extent the idea of home; a community idea of hc:ine; and
the almost boundless resources of this Jurisdiction render it possible
to carry out this idea to the fullest extent.
The Grand Master particularly urges the making of provisions
in the wills of well-to-do Masons for the expansion of the facilities
and resources of the Home establishment, and in this connection it
might be stated that not less than two magnificent bequests, each of
them amounting to possibly $100,000 or more. came to the Home within
the preceding year.
That the Home is a matter of deep interest to the brethren of this
Jurisdiction may be judged from the number of visitors which the
Horne has received in the brief time that it has been established.
For instance. in 1912, the first year that the Home was open for
visitors, the reg·istered number was 1,109.
In 1913 the number visiting the Home was 9,384, and in 1914, the
year just closed, the number was 16,014, and visitors representing many
foreign countries called and expressed their admiration and delight
at the wonderful achievements along the line of cornmunitv l'ife
established here. Some of the foreign countries represented by visitors
were England, Germany. Scotland and Australia, to say nothing of
visitors from twenty or more States of our Vnion.

activities.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Dispensations were granted within the year to form two new
Lodges. The Grand Lodge dedicated two l\fasonic halls.
The Grand Master attell(lcd on July 15 the Annnal Communication
of the Grand Lodge of Canada in Ontario, at which time a Marnnic
jubilee took place in celebration of one hundred years of peace
between England and the United States. 'fhe function was largely
attended by representatives of the Grand Cadges of Canada and the
United States.
The Grand Master reports a case of discipline which he was
called upon to enforce against one of the Subordinate Lodges, which
had refused, after :;everal requests, to conform its "work" to the
established ritual of the Grand Lodge.
This, we presume, was a case where the Lodge had inherited from
former days a form of work that differed from the established work
of the Grand Lodge. and they were loath to abandon the methods
which had been followed in the particular Lodge for so many years.
Other Grand Lodges h;1ve had the same difficulty to overcome. The
charter of the Lodge was arrested by the Grand Master. All of his
acts in connection with the case were approved by the Grand Lodge,
the charter was ordered held and the recalcitrant members of the Lodge
continued suspended from the rights and privileges of Masonry nntil
they should acknowledge their error and agree to conform strictly to
the requirements of the Grand Lodge and to its ritual; and the incoming·
Grand Master was vested with power to restore the charter when, in
his judgment, the conditions imposed by the Grand Lodge were folly
complied with.
On the second day of the Communication the Grand Chaplain
delivered a discourse upon the subject "Masonic Symbolism." That
the discourse was highly enjoyed and appreciated may he judged from
the fact that a resolution of thanks was extended to the Orator and
the Grand Secretary was instrttcted to print the Address in the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge.
The Report on Foreign Correspondence is by Jl,fost \Vorshipful
Past Grand Master E. T. D. Chambers. He holds that Masonry nmst
he justified, if at all, by service, and he feels that Masonry on this
basis does justify its existence.

VICTORIA, AUSTRALIA.
1914.

25th Annual, Melbourne, September 30.
Lodges. 212; members, 14,193; gain, 854.
In perhaps all of the Anstralian Grand
very little is brought
before the Grand Lodge except through the medium of Reports of
the Committee on General Purposes.
The Committee on General Purposes appears to be the wheel
within the wheel; in other words, the business agent to whom practically
all of the affairs of the Grand Lodge are primarily presented, and the
Grand Lodge simply registers its approval of the acts of the Committee
on General Purposes; and the Quarterly Communications of the Grand
Lodge are devoted to the consideration and approval of balance sheets
of the various Funds and of the Reports of the Committee on General
Purposes.
There is not a little to be said in favor of this method of
procedure.
Contemplated legislation and other subjects are first
thrashed out in this Committee and can only be introduced in the
Grand Lodge after consideration by it, thereby preventing a great
amount of immature and ill-considered legislation.
The Australian Jurisdictions are all characterized by splendid
business administration, and, while all of them are thrifty, possessing,
as a rule, relatively large funds, they discharge their charitable and
other ohligations in a most laudable and commendable manner. These

REPORT ON CORIUJSPONDENCE.

Jurisdictions have all adopted the system of "annuities" to dependent
Masons or orphans, and through this method the percentage of relief
is high and the cost of administration exceedingly economical, particnlarly as compared with the American ::'v1asonic Home system.
This Jurisdiction is just twcnty-fiye years old. It holds to the
credit of its various Funds an amount in excess of $200,000 and accreon.
tions to these Funds are constantly
A notable feature in connection with 1914 in this Jurisdiction was
the so-called Semi-J ubilce Celebration. In other words . the celebration
of the twenty-fifth anniversary of the founding of this Grand Lodge.
and there was printed and distributed a "Pictorial Semi-Jubilee Sounnir," which contains the pictures of all who have served as Grand
Masters and Grand Secretaries; an historical review, by l'v!ost vVorshipful Brother the Reverend A. T. Holden, Past Grand Master.
The Grand Master manifests a co~mendable pride in the Jurisdiction and recmmts the difficulties which the Grand Lodge was obliged
to fight through before it finally acquired foll rrcognition hy the Grand
Lodges of England, Ireland and Scotland, all of which had Lodges in
this territory at the time the Grand Lodge of Victoria was formed.
The information set forth in this historical review is exceedingly
interesting. It shows a gradual and substantial growth of the Grand
Lodge from· year to year; its disbursements for benevolence which have
exceeded $150,000 and other good work which it has accomplished.
In connection with the matter of
G1·and ::'vfasters in this
Turisdiction, what would strike a Mason belonging to an American
Jurisdiction as peculiar, is the manner in which they are chosen.

for
the retiring Grand Master, Most vVorshipful Brother
Holden, stated. in his Address to the Grand Lodge at the time of
the election of a new Grand Master, that there had never been any
contest for the exalted position of .Grand Master, and he .voiced the
fervent hope that there never would be. He says that the institution
stands for peace, love and harmony, and that anything that would
disturb. this placidity is against the hest interests of the Order; and
he proceeded to discuss the eligibility of proposed candidates for Grand
!\faster. and stated that, inasmuch as either himself or one other
brother must naturally he elected, he had gone into conference with
this other brother and two or three of the leading men of the Grand
Lodge, and they had d.:cidcd that the interests of the Grand Lodge
indicated the wisdom of elevating the other brother to the Grand
East. and. as a result of that conference, he virtually announced that
that brother had heen selected as Grand Master.

Four decisions were rendered by the Grand Master. The first

brewery is eligible to receive the Degrees, which is probably correct:

The second decision was to the effect that a certain Senior \Vardenelect, having a defective arm, which prevented him from assuming

properly upheld by the Jurisprudence Committee.
Another decision was to the effect that an unaffiliated l\fason,
desiring to join a Lodge, and who had loaned his dimit to a female
relative in a distant State to enable her to join the Order of Eastern

his <limit, but that the original dimit must of necessity accompany the

under the laws of California, if he could prove the copy. it would be
accepted in lieu of the original.
Recognition was extended to the Grand Lodge of Costa.Rica.

"The Book of Constitutions, for us the Bible, is a part of Masonry;
and every tenet of the Fraternity is found in that blessed volume. From
the Jirst it is the rnle and guide of our faith. I have heard Masons sav
that l\fasonry was a good enough church for them. Be warned at this
point. Let no one rest his eternal welfare on this fallacy. Masonry is
not the church. !mt in Christian lands it is the hand-maiden of the
church. It tracks cxactlv in the line of Bible l\1orality; but this is not
sectarianism. Y ct I regard it just as necessary for my eternal welfare
that I should belong to the church of my choice, although Masonry is
built upon the morality of the Holy Scriptures.

"X o, my brethren, !VIasonry is not a mere system of ritualism. It
teaches more than a mere philosophy; it teaches us that the trne and
faithful l\iason is the son of God. and it doth not yet appear what he
shall he."

\Vorshipful George \V. Atkinson, Past Grand Master.

In his Conclusion, he gives expression to his opinion that, so far
as he is able to judge, Freemasonry throughout the world is going
forward with steady steps and stately mien, and is apparently impregnable against any attacks made upon it. "The mustard-seed shot of
her opponents," he remarks, "have thus far fallen harmlessly at her
feet."

cation was the consideration of the Home proposition, and the adoption

We have made something of a study of Masonic Hom es and
heartily approve of the system in Jurisdictions that arc able, without.
distress, to carry the projects forward, and \Visconsin is. one of the
Jurisdictions that is large enough numerically, and enthusiastic enough

personally, we are clclightecl to sec \Visconsin falling into line in the

upon the score of economy. Masonic Homes do not afford an economic
means of taking care of aged and decrepit 2\Iasons and the widows and
orphans of Masons, but it docs, we believe. afford the best way of
accomplishing this work, and we arc sure that in J urisclictions that
do not have these institutions many of those who are entitled to this
kind of relief are overlooked entirely, and in Masonry, as in everything
else, perhaps more especially in Masonry, one is helped by helping
others.
